entry.title: My Son’s Favorite Screen-Free Activity Is a Cassette Tape
entry.summary: It’s cheaper than a Yoto.
entry.content:
Most afternoons around 4 o’clock, my 7-year old son disappears into his room and I hear a sound I haven’t heard in 30 years: the clink of a cassette door closing, the hiss of a tape rewinding, and then the crackly, fuzzy, warbly sound of a British man’s voice introducing the title of a story.

Yes, these are audio cassettes, and they have quietly changed what independent play looks like in our house. Like most millennials, I spent my early childhood in a time before Audible, before podcasts, even before MP3s. I had a vast library of children’s tapes, and some of my most comforting memories are of lying on my bed on 110th Street, nodding off to Richard Scarry’s Bedtime Stories.

My kids have full bookshelves and we read together every night before bed. But that is different from what I had with my tapes. Listening to them was something I did on my own without a grown-up in the room. It symbolized independence, privacy, and self-sufficiency, and I wanted him to have that too.

Friends suggested the Yoto, but something about it wasn’t for me. It’s expensive. A full-size player costs $150, and story cards have to be bought individually for around $13 each. And the Yoto is still another smart device, more like a terminal than a toy, and it comes along with (predictably) an optional subscription.

It occurred to me that what I wanted for him actually existed, it just had to be bought secondhand. So I set off on an eBay quest. I thought of all the books I’d loved as a kid and began filling a virtual cart with classics, from The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to Harriet the Spy to Matilda. One by one they arrived in our mailbox, some in chunky plastic clamshells, others in flimsy cardboard sleeves, the rest in clear plastic cases with at least one broken hinge.

He was hooked. Like Max in Where the Wild Things Are whose bedroom sprouts up a forest, my son found his room turning into a wardrobe to Narnia, a boat ride on Willy Wonka’s chocolate river, a trip to Neverland. And like Max, when the adventure ended, it was time for dinner.

What surprised me was how obsessed he became with the mechanical aspects of the cassettes. It took him a minute to learn which button did what, but I could tell immediately that he loved the feeling of popping open the cassette player and flipping the tape over when one side ended. If a part was too scary, he fast-forwarded it. If he missed something, he would rewind and listen again. I watched as he developed greater fine motor control, patience with small mechanical tasks, and a sense of order, reading labels and counting to make sure the right tapes were in the right boxes in the right order.

It took us a few tries to find the right cassette player. Cheap portable models broke easily and chewed through batteries. A boom box I liked for its 1990s design arrived cute but nonfunctional. Then we found the QFX Retro-38BT, a solar-powered, rechargeable shoe-box tape recorder. It’s a tank and has survived being dropped, stepped on, and carried around the house by its handle. It’s a radio in case he ever wants to listen to a game on WFAN, and it also records, which means one day he can make mixtapes of his own.

There is some science behind why tapes might be good for kids. In a 1988 UCLA cognitive study, researchers found that children who heard a story on audiotape invented more original endings than kids who watched the same story as a cartoon, proving a theory that audio asks kids to put in more “high mental effort” imagining the story visually in their mind.

Like anything with kids, tapes can go from a habit to an obsession, so we try to keep it to an hour a day. After that hour, he comes out of his room, blinking, back from wherever he’s been, and asks what’s for dinner.

Pro tip: The narrators are just as important as the stories! For example, you can listen to Paul Newman, Sidney Poitier, Kathleen Turner, and Matthew Broderick read D’Aulaires’ Book of Greek Myths.

entry.title: The Best Items to Stock for Any Emergency, According to Survivalists
entry.summary: Whether you’re bugging out or bugging in, these are the things you may want to have on hand.
entry.content:
Compiling a stash of emergency-preparedness items used to be a task many of us kept on the back burner — something we knew was important and we’d get to eventually. But eventually, we now know, might be closer than anyone thought. And while we’re not suggesting you start digging out an underground bunker and filling it with instant noodles, in the past few years we’ve come to learn that having a few things on hand before you need them will only help you, even if it’s just mentally.

Most preppers, like Oregon’s Afrovivalist, Sharon Ross, equate preparation with peace of mind. “Once a person is prepared during a disaster,” she says, “they don’t feel the sense of urgency to go shopping for supplies.” So if visions of empty store shelves still haunt you, have a nice, calm look at our well-organized, detailed list of emergency supplies to keep on hand. To assemble it, we consulted recommendations from the CDC, Red Cross, the Department of Homeland Security, and the NYC Emergency Management Department. But those agencies give you only general categories, and we wanted specifics. So we interviewed 22 survivalists, preppers, bushcrafters, homesteaders, and emergency professionals about their favorite things to always have on-hand — and their advice to make your bugout (or bugin) the best it can possibly be.

Here are their suggestions, broken down into categories based on your level of survivalist instinct. There’s a lot to sift through here, but you can pick and mix products according to your needs. For many, a leaner survival kit makes more sense than a military-grade one. “Simplicity is key when prepping,” says Prepper Press founder Derrick James. Especially as, in a worst-case scenario, you might have to haul all of this gear a considerable distance. “It’s really important for people to know what their limitations are,” says emergency preparedness expert Aton Edwards, author of the book Preparedness Now! “Don’t prove how strong you are by dragging around a 40-pound bag. Rage lift in the gym, don’t rage lift your bag.” And in any potential urban or wilderness survival situation, advises Steve Lancia of North Camp Survival School in the Hudson Valley, there’s one piece of gear you should always keep around: “A cool head.”

Updated on October 28, 2026
We’ve updated this list to make sure our top emergency picks are still available and correctly priced.

If you’re not quite ready to build your own bunker, check out our first-timers’ guide to getting prepared:

Most preppers keep two bags: a three-day bag and a two-week bag. While you needn’t get too hung up on that, it’s not a terrible idea to have something that you can easily grab that has everything you need in it in case you have to leave quickly. Bushcrafter Mark Christensen recommends a “quality rucksack, or even a five-gallon bucket, which keeps your emergency gear together.” Survivalist E.J. “Skullcrusher” Snyder (whom you might know from his many appearances on Naked and Afraid) likes the “tough and roomy” bags by Gregory, but if you prefer something more tactical, he suggests something by Maxpedition. Jim Cobb, editor-in-chief of Prepper Survival Guide and Backwoods Survival Guide magazines, likes the RUSH24 bag from 5.11 Tactical, saying that it’s “robust without being ridiculously huge.” And Lisa Bedford, a.k.a. the Survival Mom, loves the Presidio Tactical Assault Backpack from Flying Circle, because it’s “a very good size for teens and most women.”

Edwards suggests an alternative to traditional rucksacks: the humble folding shopping cart. “If you aren’t physically fit, then lugging around a fully stocked go-bag can be difficult,” he explains. “So a folding cart will let you move around from one shelter to another shelter.”

Survivalist Travis McGill, along with Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools, and a survivalist who asked that we refer to him by the pseudonym “RC” like Surefire flashlights because they’re virtually indestructible. They’re so durable, in fact, that some are specially designed to be used as a self-defense weapon, Coyne says. McGill uses the Surefire D3ft but admits “it’s totally overkill” and says you could also “get something that takes AA or AAA batteries since they’re easy to find and replace.” Even a small one for your keychain will do, says Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army special forces captain and author of several survival books. “But make sure it has a turn on button, not just squeeze on, for when you need to have light to work and be hands free,” he says. Cobb, Edwards, Snyder and Morgan Rogue of the prepper site Rogue Preparedness, however, prefer headlamps to flashlights so you can be 100 percent hands-free and there’s less chance you’ll put your torch down and lose it. Rogue likes Foxelli or Petzl, while Snyder uses a Black Diamond Spot 325. Cobb also pointed us toward Streamlight’s products, which “work very well and will take a beating.”

There was plenty of consensus here, too. Unsurprisingly, everyone likes a Leatherman, a brand that also came out strong on our list of the best multi-tools. “I am a big fan,” Snyder says. “There are many types to choose from to meet your needs and budget.” Coyne likes the Supertool 300. And John Ramey of the prepper site theprepared.com likes the Leatherman Wave+ because it “doesn’t waste space and weight on tools that don’t matter much in an emergency, but it’s versatile and robust enough to be a core survival item.” The Signal, which McGill uses, also includes a fire starter and a whistle. If your survival budget doesn’t stretch to Leatherman, Lancia pointed us to the more affordable knife brand SOG, which designs similarly compact multi-tools for half the price.

For most preppers, recommending a first-aid kit off the shelf would be like Julia Child telling you her favorite flavor of Pop-Tart. They like to put them together themselves so they can pack them with, as Hawke puts it, “some dressings for real trauma,” including tourniquets, Israeli Bandages, and, in R.C.’s case, zip-tie restraints, though he wouldn’t really say what those were for. That said, Coyne calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best first-aid kits on the market [and] definitely the closest commercially available to what I would customize for myself.” Survival Mom has a different preference, saying, “it would be hard to find better medical kits than those sold by Dr. Joe and Amy Alton at Doom & Bloom.” Their company offers a variety of kits that cover everything from labor to gunshot wounds. Whatever first aid kid you decide on, Mike Glover, crisis management and response expert and host of the popular FieldCraft Survival podcast, recommends you always maintain a 30-day supply of over-the-counter medicine (like painkillers, cold, allergy, anti-diarrheal medications) as well as any prescription medications. And another consideration, via Edwards: “There should be stuff for dental emergencies as well. Any kind of emergency that forces you to evacuate, especially in the city, you’re not going to be able to find a dentist.”

Most of our experts recommended Kaito shortwave radios. Coyne’s favorite is the Kaito Voyager because it’s rugged and water-resistant, has plug-in and solar charging capabilities, and is shortwave, which means it picks up broadcasts from around the world. “In an extreme global situation, an entire country may be off-grid, but someone, somewhere, will be broadcasting,” Hawke says. Edwards agrees that a hand-crank radio is vital: “You don’t know if the internet and cellular networks are going to work.” Snyder likes the Kaito KA500 Emergency Radio. “It’s capable of being charged via hand crank, solar panel, micro USB, a standard wall outlet, or batteries,” he says. “And it has a five-LED reading lamp, an LED flashlight, and a red LED SOS beacon light.”

Waterproof matches are the best matches, though our experts say lighters are better than matches. Rogue recommends carrying both, in case either fails. Edwards, Cobb, and Hawke like Bic lighters, but Hawke stresses that “folks should review fire basics [because] it’s surprising how many people don’t know how to build a fire once they have a light.” Coyne uses only UCO Stormproof matches. “Once lit, they cannot be put out,” he says. “They even burn underwater.”

Hawke, Coyne, and R.C. all recommend power banks (which can be used to charge phones and other devices) that can be charged by multiple sources, including the sun. While Coyne personally uses a (now sold-out) Kodiak brand power bank because it’s rugged, water resistant, and has an emergency light, he recommends several reliable options that will also jump start your car, and are extremely small, such as the NOCO Boost. (Coyne also likes OtterBox’s charging cables because they’re “super strong” and “won’t rip or tear easily.”)

Ramey is the one naysayer when it comes to devices that use solar panels. He prefers to avoid them, because “you don’t want your battery baking in the sun,” he says. After “deep field testing,” he recommends the Anker PowerCore 10,000mAh. He calls it “the right mix of ruggedness, size and weight, capacity, and performance.” Rogue also likes “anything by Anker” to “charge your phone or other devices perfectly.”

Coyne uses only Energizer, and Ramey won’t budge from his Panasonic Eneloops “because they last a long time sitting on a shelf,” and Survival Mom loves the ones from Survival Frog (no relation). One thing all of our experts agree on is that whatever batteries you get, they should be rechargeable.

R.C. likes anything from The North Face. Coyne prefers the Montbell brand. Unlike mummy-style bags, which taper toward the bottom like mummy wrappings, Montbells stretch and are “next-level comfortable,” he says. Hawke recommends a slightly more austere (and multipurpose) solution: “a large trash bag, like 55-gallon type, can serve as great sleeping bag, shelter, rucksack, float, etc.”

No big surprise here: Everyone likes wool. Get “a good, old-fashioned wool blanket,” says Snyder, because it’s “tough, breathes well, and keeps you warm, even if it gets wet.” He suggests an Army–issued wool blanket from a military surplus store. RC loves Pendelton, and Coyne likes the Jungle Blanket by Snugpak. He calls it “a next-level woobie” (military slang for blanket) because it’s “warm, compressible, and water resistant.” If you have any extras around and are stuck at home without heat, Survival Mom also recommends covering the windows of your smallest room with blankets to stay warm.

Edwards says you shouldn’t underestimate the power of a good night’s sleep in a stressful situation. Alongside a good blanket, “what’s nice to have is an inflatable hiking pillow,” he explains. “One of the most important things you need to do in a crisis is get sleep, because your body gets worn down because of the stress it’s under.”

A surprising number of emergency checklists suggest bringing a puzzle to give yourself something fun to do. But “forget the puzzle,” Coyne says. “A deck of cards is best.” Hawke agrees, preferring cards for their small size, portability, and the numerous games that can be played with them. Also, as they both point out, you can get cards with survival info on the back, turning your diversion into a mini cheat sheet. And don’t forget to bring toys for your kids, Edwards says, “because they’re going to be frightened.” Cobb suggests a family-friendly board game that will keep everyone distracted and entertained during power outages: “Having a couple of fun board games or something similar will go a long way to keeping everyone busy and their minds off the crisis at hand for a bit.”

Bleach isn’t the only cleaner that will do the job. Snyder says cleaners like Lysol and Pine-Sol also work to keep things “germ free so that everyone stays healthy and doesn’t get sick.” But if you like bleach, any unscented, unadulterated bleach is fine. “Just get some bleach,” R.C. says.

Now hear us out: It might sound extreme, but at some point, you’ll probably wish you had some food. Our experts all approach the food question a little differently. Homesteader Lisa Sutton and the popular YouTuber, Prepper Potpourri (both Michiganers, both grandmothers), are big fans of canning and dehydrating. These processes take a little know-how, but are ultimately very practical and sustainable, especially if you grow your own food. They both like the All American Canner and the Excalibur Dehydrator. If you’re not ready to make your own food, our experts recommend stocking your pantry with, ideally, two-weeks’ worth of non-perishable foods like canned and dried goods, and peanut butter. “Think of very very simple meals, like oatmeal, [and] meals where you can open up a can of soup or chili and pour it over the rice and have more calories and more servings,” says Survival Mom, who goes into more detail about this in her book. And make sure you get stuff you actually like: “Don’t stock up on beans and rice if you don’t eat beans and rice,” Sutton says. Cobb’s in agreement: “Store what you eat and eat what you store. Don’t go out and buy cases of special ‘survival food’ if that’s not what you’re eating normally — a disaster or emergency is the last place you want to add stomach upset to the mix.” 

If you want more variety and are thinking of supplementing your stock with freeze-dried food, Survival Mom, Prepper Potpourri, and David at Preppers Survive like Mountainhouse. Sutton recommends products from Thrive Life, “because they are real food, not prepackaged, high carb, high sodium emergency foods” like typical emergency foods tend to be. Hawke likes MRE’s (which aren’t technically freeze dried and which civilians can now buy), beef jerky, and meals from a company called Wise Foods, whose empty containers, he suggests, can be used as toilets. And don’t forget condiments, he says. R.C. recommends any junk food since it’s “full of sugar and preservatives and is good for survival,” if nothing else. Rogue suggests “morale-boosting foods” like macaroni and cheese, packaged cookies, raisins, dehydrated fruits, popcorn, and chocolate. And Edwards points us toward “high-protein stuff that’s not very heavy” like energy bars and trail mix. “Because when you’re in a crisis situation, you are going to burn more energy than you normally expend.”

Jessica Kellog of the City of Los Angeles Emergency Management Department recommends having one gallon of water per person per day for seven days, but R.C. suggests getting even more: “You can’t have too much water,” he says. “If disaster strikes, the first thing I would do is fill the bathtub or the sink with water to keep it as a reserve.” As Edwards points out, “any kind of emergency where you have to evacuate your home, especially in a city, would probably classify as something that would disrupt water treatment.” If you’re sticking to bottled, any kind will do. But once that’s gone, you need to have a way to resupply, says Hawke. There are many ways to purify water. The easiest ways are by boiling (you’ll need something metal in which to do that), with water purification tablets (Coyne likes these), and through various filtration systems. Hawke likes the Life Straw and the O-Zone Pen for individual use, and Rogue, Prepper Potpourri, and Survival Mom like a Berkey for something bigger. David likes LifeStraw’s one-gallon gravity bag that removes lead, parasites, bacteria, and chemicals. It can also be used as a straw alone, with a plastic bottle, or with in-line hydration bladders. If you need a smaller option, Survival Mom uses and recommends the Sawyer Mini. Edwards agrees that the Sawyer is “a really good filter, that’s one of the easiest and smallest to use.” 

Even if you have the ability to filter water on the go, Edwards says that in an emergency, “you’ll want to be carrying as many containers as you can.” James says that these Aquabricks are “the best semi-portable water storage containers” he’s seen. “They’re strong, very stackable, and come with an optional water-filtration system.”

The consensus seems to be for Heatsheets, which our experts say are the strongest and lightest options available. “There are more lightweight ones, but they rip easily,” says Coyne. McGill suggests getting this option, which is sized for two, making it easier to stay covered.

“Just get the loudest,” says Coyne, who also recommends whistles “without moving parts,” like this one.

Rogue says that hand warmers like these are a godsend, and Survival Mom likes this rechargeable, handheld option from Frog & Co. Or, for a more long-term solution, James suggests simply investing in “a decent pair of warm gloves.”

“When thinking of an emergency that would force New Yorkers to evacuate — like an earthquake — masks are important because there would be an enormous amount of particulate in the air, infused with toxic materials,” says Edwards. He, Coyne and Rogue suggest N-95 masks, which paramedics use to protect themselves from pathogens. Ross, on the other hand, suggests you go for a reusable P-100 respirator, which offers the highest protection possible, blocking out 99.9 percent of contaminants, compared to an N-95, which filters out just 95 percent of particles and isn’t oil-resistant. Lancia says it isn’t so paranoid to buy a full-face mask (“The more I watch the news, the more I’m convinced that we all need a high-quality gas mask and CBRN filter to go with it. Mira Safety makes some of the best.”) But, as Christensen points out, “even a wet rag held over your mouth and nose helps a lot.” For extra preparedness points: “I would also have goggles to protect my eyes,” says Edwards. “And I’d have work gloves in there, because in the case of an earthquake, you’re moving debris.”

There are four different classes of fire extinguishers for four different kinds of fires — ordinary combustibles, grease, electrical, and metal — and our guess is you’d rather not get them all. (For example, R.C. likes a sleek Blaze Defense Fire Suppression Device, but it’s not for use on electrical fires.) Your best bet is a standard home model, which is versatile and inexpensive.

“Every household needs at least one alternative way to warm and cook food and heat water, and a solar cooker doesn’t require storing any type of fuel, which is a huge advantage,” says Survival Mom, who recommends a simple, box-style model. She also likes rocket stoves, “highly efficient stoves that require only tiny amounts of biofuel,” like the EcoZoom Dual Fuel model. David prefers Coughlin’s steel-coated canned-heat stove, which is sturdy enough for heavy pots and has covered sides that block wind. It’s compatible with any canned fuel and folds flat when not in use.

Should you find yourself at home without heat, “seal off one room that has the fewest number of windows or anything that’s gonna allow cold air to come in, and put up a tent in that room,” says Survival Mom. A cold-weather tent like this one is a good choice, she says, since it’s both warm and small enough to fit in a small room.

“Plastic sheeting, or even a nice tarp, can have many uses: from collecting rain water to drink, to [making] a traveling shelter if you don’t have a tent [and] sealing off areas to keep out germs or bad air from coming in,” Snyder says. Edwards also recommends tarps as a tent alternative: “A tarp can provide a barrier from the ground, or become a shelter — tents can be a little expensive, and tarps are tougher.”

Snyder calls duct tape “a survivalist’s best friend” that he’s seen used for “everything from making cups to helping stabilize a broken limb to patching leaks.” He and Coyne both like Gorilla tape. Alongside duct tape, Edwards says you can “never have too much line” for tying things down, and recommends carrying a fair few feet of versatile paracord. Cobb agrees, saying that paracord is “the traditional cordage for preppers.”

Everyone recommends you have a plan, preferably written out, and, if not rehearsed, at least talked about and memorized by everyone in your family. “Because in those moments when you’re frozen in indecision, and you panic, you’re starting to make really bad decisions,” says Survival Mom, who explains that “what you put into place beforehand is going to help you make the best decisions in those very intense moments.” “To implement the plan,” says Kellog, “survival supplies should be stored in accessible places that are known to members within the household,” And you should know how and when to use all the items you’ve gathered and test all your gear. And be sure to store important documents, photos and other items all in one place. Rogue suggests a fireproof and waterproof bag for this purpose. Edwards adds that when on the move, you’ll want to keep those passports and birth certificates close to your person, rather than in a separate bug-out bag.

Hawke loves these and has found over thirty uses for them, examples of which are here and here.

Glover recommends that “people carry a stockpile of personal hygiene items in the event infrastructure and supply chains are adversely affected.” Both Rogue and David like alcohol-free No-Rinse Body Wash. And rather than carrying a stockpile of toilet paper, Edwards suggests packing a travel bidet, which will take up less space and be “a lot more sanitary.” In general, he says, “don’t short yourself” on these kinds of comfort items. “Because you want to be able to maintain your sanity. These are the little things that keep you sane.”

Have a compass and a mirror (Coyne likes this one, below), and designate FEMA locations and evacuation routes on your map.

Ross recommends you educate yourself about what you can and can’t eat out in the wild and suggests you get a book on the subject.

“For waste disposal,” Kellog says.

McGill suggests getting a 2000W generator like this one to keep in the garage in suburban areas so you can keep your refrigerator on and charge your phones in case of power outages.

McGill also suggests keeping five gallons of gas in your garage. “To keep it from going bad, you can fill your car up with it once a month and take the tank to get refilled with fresh fuel at the gas station.”

Rogue swears by a folding portable solar panel “that you can open up and place within sunlight to charge your devices directly from the panel,” she says. “They come with USB plugs, so phones and other devices plug right in. You can do it outside or through a sunny window.” Goal Zero panels have never failed her, “and they’ll even work with some overcast, which is rare with the smaller solar panels.”

Survival Mom recommends having a solar light and prefers a collapsible one, “so it can be tucked into a backpack, glove box, or any other small area.”

If you’re worried about the possibility of a nuclear electromagnetic pulse event — the likes of which could potentially short-circuit your personal electronic equipment, and came up in conversation with many of the preppers we talked to — then James suggests investing in Faraday protection for your all-important phone and laptop.

entry.title: On My Mind: All the Ways I Retinol
entry.summary: Our beauty writer is slathering herself in face, neck, and body retinoids.
entry.content:
During the pandemic, I started consistently using prescription tretinoin. It faded my freckles, a benefit I hadn’t anticipated, but the persistent dryness and flaking led me to switch to an over-the-counter retinal, which helped maintain my results with less irritation. (I wrote about my experience with a retinal cream from K-beauty brand Celimax here.)

Now that I’m 46, fine lines and dark spots aren’t my biggest concerns; skin laxity is, particularly on my lower face and neck. I attended a launch event for Cottonball, a new customized prescription-skin-care brand back in September. The brand takes into account the products you already use, climate, sensitivity, skin type and tone, and health history to tailor tretinoin formula (it adds in other ingredients, such as hyaluronic acid, ceramides, bakuchiol, tranexamic acid, and niacinamide). Mine arrived as two prescriptions, one for my face and one for my neck, with a lower concentration of tretinoin in the latter.

So far, the adjustment has been surprisingly easy: I’ve experienced a little flaking on my neck, almost none on my face, and no significant irritation or initial breakout (often called a purge). My skin already looks smooth and brighter, but it’s too early to judge longer-term firming results. For now, I’m sticking with it.

I’m also looking beyond my face. As I’ve noticed more cellulite on my thighs, I’m wondering whether thinning body skin might be making the dimpling more apparent. Because retinoids are among the few topical ingredients with evidence of stimulating collagen production, body-retinol creams have caught my attention, too.

Dermatologist Kavita Mariwalla, MD, explained that results on the body may take much longer than on the face because body skin is thicker. Still, I’m willing to give them a shot.

I’ve been using Nécessaire’s Body Retinol nightly, and I love how smooth it leaves my skin. It’s also fragrance-free, a major plus for me since fragranced body products sometimes trigger hives. I haven’t experienced any irritation or flaking.

This one pairs retinol with ceramides and a copper peptide for additional firming benefits. It’s really lightweight and absorbs quickly.

I’ve always loved Josie Maran’s body butters. The consistencies are so good and leave my skin so smooth and well moisturized. This one has retinol derived from lab-grown algae and also contains the brand’s signature argan oil.

Working at the Strategist has made me realize I’m just not fussy enough about my bedding. I get decent sleep, but my sheets are basic, my pillows are nothing special, and my comforter could use an upgrade. I’ll start with some new sheets — higher thread count and a soft, buttery sateen finish.

I’ve also been basic with Advent calendars over the years. Our elf has always bought the old-school cardboard calendars with the chocolates on December 1. But our Advent-calendar roundups at the Strategist have me tempted to step it up this year with more fun calendars. entry.title: I Interviewed Over a Dozen Teens About Fragrances. They Want These Scents.
entry.summary: Gen Z’s holiday wish lists might just be harder to parse than ever — at least when it comes to fragrance.
entry.content:
Brett, a 15-year-old who lives in Washington, bought his first fragrance the summer before eighth grade on a recommendation from a friend. He wore the now-discontinued bottle from Pacsun for All for about a year. “Then I started seeing videos on TikTok about how if you want to have better hygiene, you have to invest in yourself and get fragrances,” he told me. “I started looking up what fragrances I should get, and I went down this rabbit hole.” He came out of it with four new colognes — Yves Saint Laurent Y Eau de Parfum, Emporio Armani Stronger With You Intensely, Valentino Born in Roma Coral Fantasy, and Versace Dylan Blue — all of which are favorites on #PerfumeTok. Two years after he bought the Pacsun scent, Brett started his own TikTok account dedicated to his fragrance collection, which now includes 11 bottles, with several more on his wish list. He’s among the growing number of teens going all in on their signature scent.

Gen Z’s fascination with fragrance is nothing new. Tweens made headlines back in 2024 for raiding the Sol de Janeiro displays at Sephora (and, famously, Drunk Elephant’s too), and in 2025, The Cut reported that the main target of the perfume industry is Gen Z. We’ve since seen teens popularize the terms “smellmaxxing” (enhancing your own scent) and “scent layering” (combining scented lotions with perfumes and other fragrances). This all compounds into holiday wish lists that might just be harder to parse than ever — at least when it comes to fragrance.

So if you’re a parent who just received a wish list packed with bottles from LoveShackFancy, Billie Eilish, and Kayali (or Valentino, YSL, and Armani, for the boys), it might feel impossible to know where to start. To help make sense of the requests — and to understand what to buy and what to skip — I chatted with over a dozen teens about the scents they wear every day and are hoping to receive this holiday season. Below, everything I learned.

They were raised on Sol de Janeiro’s salted-caramel “62” body mist, and as they’ve grown older, their tastes haven’t shifted much. “I love sweet scents. Sweet, feminine, girly,” 18-year-old Ellie Carpenter from the U.K. says, and over in Florida, 17-year-old Kamila agrees. “I do gravitate toward those sweet scents, especially now since we’re reaching the fall and winter,” she says. The boys notice it too: “The note that I smell the most in classrooms is vanilla, and that’s because the girls shower themselves in vanilla,” says 21-year-old Jason Lagos. They’re spritzing fragrances from Kayali, Billie Eilish, and LoveShackFancy (more on those later), but they’ve also leveled up their Sol de Janeiro: 16-year-old Naomi from Canada has the eau de parfum version of the famous 62 mist on her holiday wish list.

Perhaps the most asked-for scents are a couple of gourmand fragrances from Kayali called Yum Boujee Marshmallow and Vanilla 28. “I mostly just see influencers talk about it, saying it’s really good, so that has influenced me into wanting to buy it,” Ellie told me. “People say that it smells like straight vanilla extract, so I’m really intrigued.”

No one seems to know how to describe the different-on-everyone scent, but Glossier’s signature You fragrance is still a staple in three of the teens’ scent wardrobes, especially for school. “It’s very soft and subtle, so it’s not overpowering,” Kamila says. “A lot of people compliment it just because it smells more natural, rather than a more pungent, powerful scent that can often trigger allergies.”

Has any brand done as many collaborations this year as LoveShackFancy? Gracie, 15, from Oklahoma sleeps in its bedding (a collaboration with Pottery Barn) and has one of the LoveShackFancy Lola Blankets on her wish list. She first bought the brand’s Secret Crush perfume as a decoration piece for her room. “Then I was like, Okay, well, it smells really good too. It’s just perfect,” she told me. Gracie, like many other girls I chatted with, has the brand’s vanilla Secret Crush perfume. “They’re not crazy expensive, but also you don’t need a lot of product for it to smell very strong, so they last a while,” says 17-year-old Camryn, who has Secret Crush and a summery fragrance called Love on the Beach on her wish list.

Billie Eilish’s vanilla eau de parfum and Ariana Grande’s floral Mod Blush were favorites last year, and they were still popular with most of the girls I chatted with. There’s also a new contender from Tate McRae that’s fresh and woody, with notes of bergamot, sage, and amber — a rare non-vanilla scent for Gen Z. It’s been out for only a month, and it’s already one of the top-ten most requested gifts on Giftful, teens’ favorite wish-list-making app.

Like many an aughts item, Victoria’s Secret’s perfume mists are back on wish lists this year. While the fruity-floral Love Spell was the pick of the ’00s, now it’s another vanilla scent, Bare Vanilla, that teens are coveting. (It’s another regular on Giftful’s “Top 100 Trending”.) Other favorites include the passion-fruit-forward and vanilla body spray called Warm and Cozy and the sweet and floral Tease eau de parfum.

Fragrances from Altar’d State and Pacsun also came up in my conversations. Fifteen-year-old Kristen from Minnesota is most intrigued by Altar’d State’s Sunkissed body mist, which smells like coconut and vanilla. “A few of my friends have some of their scents, and I always notice that it smells really good,” she says.

Most of the time, teens aren’t buying fragrances directly from the brand. Sephora is, unsurprisingly, one of their favorite places to shop for and sniff new fragrances, but they’re also going to Target, which recently launched its Beauty Studio, a “destination for what’s new, now and next in beauty” — including fragrance. “I feel like every time I’m there, there’s always something new or something I’ve heard about, so I like to try them out sometimes, and I feel like for the most part they’re really good,” says Kristen. When they shop there, teens are buying fragrances from Frenshe, EOS, Athena Club, and Dossier.

Just last month, Brett got a bottle of Valentino’s Born in Roma Uomo Extradose for $115 — rather than $190 — on Aura Fragrances. It’s one of the many discount retailers that teens regularly shop at to afford their fragrance wardrobes. Some of the teens I chatted with mentioned others — like Beauty House, Arvella Fragrance, and Fragrance.Net — but the discounts don’t mean they’re buying blind. “You go into these fragrance stores and they’re helping you out like, Oh what do you want to smell? What do you want to buy? But you’re just there to smell it to make sure that you like it, so that you can buy it online,” Lagos says.

Dupes — especially those from Dossier — came up with a couple of the girls I chatted with. (The brand’s ambery vanilla scent — you guessed it — is a favorite.) It was the boys, though, that have been experimenting with a long list of brands specializing in what many of the teens called “inspired-by fragrances.” Jay, 15, owns about 40 dupes and says, “It’s just an easy way to expand your taste.” There are several TikTok famous dupe brands, including Mykonos, which Jay says is so good the scents often sell out instantly, and Rayhaan, whose most famous scent is a dupe of Creed’s Virgin Island Water. According to Eduardo, a 17-year-old fragrance head from Florida, the dupes just keep getting better. “And they’re getting faster,” too, he says. “Parfums De Marly Althair Exclusif came out like a couple weeks ago. I’m already seeing dupes for it.”

Still, not everyone is pro-dupe. Whenever Lagos makes videos about dupe fragrances, he says people call him a “dupe demon.” Sixteen-year-old Liam, who recently started his own perfume brand, is staunchly against them. “I feel that dupes almost take away from the hobby and undermine people’s hard work by just copying them and selling them at a lower price tag.”

For teens like Liam who go for the real deal, it’s all about the big four: Yves Saint Laurent, Valentino, Jean Paul Gaultier, and Emporio Armani. Almost like clockwork, just about every teenage boy I interviewed mentioned at least one fragrance from each of the fragrance houses. Nineteen-year-old Jackson Shoop says that Jean Paul Gaultier’s Le Male Elixir, an amber-forward fragrance with notes of lavender and tonka bean, is the most well-known fragrance among teenage boys right now. Based on my conversations with teens, I don’t doubt that to be true, but I also heard about YSL’s Y eau de parfum, Armani’s Stronger With You Intensely, and Valentino’s Born in Roma Coral Fantasy more times than I can count. (Some girls, like Kristen, like the feminine version of Valentino’s Born in Roma, too.)

There’s a smellmaxxing aspect to fragrance layering, but there’s also a practical reason for doing it: “Moisturizing is the most important thing to do before you put on a fragrance,” Lagos says. “I like to moisturize to just give better projection and better longevity to my fragrance.” He and Brett both use lotions from EOS, which are also popular with the girls.

For girls, though, scent layering includes complementary body mists, hair perfumes, body washes, body lotions, and sometimes even leave-in conditioners. Some teens, like Kristen and 17-year-old Jordan, put on scented lotion after every shower to complement whatever fragrance they plan to wear the next day. Jordan says, “Sometimes I don’t know what people are complimenting me on because I layer a lot of my scents.”

entry.title: Murdle Stopped Me From Doomscrolling
entry.summary: A couple of puzzles a day has stopped my mindless scrolling.
entry.content:
I’ve tried all kinds of strategies to get my screen time down. I got a Hatch to banish my phone from the bedroom at night, set time limits on my apps (easily bypassed), and swapped my nighttime scroll for a Kobo. All of these strategies have made some impact, but nothing has been as effective at tearing me away from my finely tuned algorithm as Murdle. The logic game started online but has since evolved into a book with many editions. I bought my first one last year at Book Culture in Long Island City. It was placed conspicuously on a shelf, and I picked it up out of curiosity because it rhymed with Wordle, a game I play daily. I flipped through and within 30 seconds added it to my pile. I went home and played the first puzzle. Then another. I’ve long been a fan of logic games to the point that I once considered taking the LSAT when I learned logic games were part of the test. I enjoy the dopamine hit of solving a problem, especially one with many possible solutions. The feeling is not totally dissimilar to scrolling on Instagram and finding a delightful Reel or sinking an hour or so into Threads. I’m also paranoid about my brain atrophying, so I figured this was a low-cost way for me to stave off mental decline. What I didn’t expect is that it would become a regular part of my routine.

Every puzzle starts with a murder for Deductive Logico to solve. There are a few clues and a list of possible suspects, locations, and murder weapons. It’s like lots of mini-games of Clue. Each edition of Murdle has 100 puzzles. Those are separated by difficulty, which helps to avoid the monotony of the puzzles becoming easy. Even the easier puzzles can be difficult — I recently bought the second edition of the book and found myself sitting for a while in a coffee shop trying to figure out what I was missing. Typically, each puzzle takes me about five or so minutes to solve, faster if I employ the help of my wife. It’s about the same amount of time I scroll in the middle of the day when my brain wants a break from a more important task. While it hasn’t replaced my feed by any stretch of the imagination, it creates some space between me and my phone.

It’s worked so well for me that I plan on buying a few copies for friends this holiday season, many of whom are trying to get their screen time down too. It’s much cheaper than a Brick and easy to whip out while in transit. It also trains your brain to associate idle time with something other than scrolling. While an app blocker essentially gives you back your time by stopping the reward cycle of getting on Instagram or TikTok, it doesn’t really offer a suggestion for what to do with however many minutes you’ve wrestled back. Murdle has proved to be a solid solution.

entry.title: Rita Konig’s Favorite Under-$100 Home Items
entry.summary: Wicker drink koozies, strawberry hullers, and trays for giant ice cubes.
entry.content:
Design can be prohibitively expensive, but not far from, say, Julianne Moore’s George Nakashima table there might just be a solid, economical Ikea shelf. In this series, we ask designers for their favorite useful, utilitarian home items under a hundred dollars. This week, London-based designer Rita Konig, who just launched Rita Konig Household Goods, her first home-wares collection, shares her essential wicker drink koozie, strawberry huller, and tray for giant ice cubes.

When I moved back to London in 2012 after six years in New York, I bought a small flat on the far edge of Notting Hill and made it the perfect bachelorette pad: a large sitting room, a small bedroom, and a genuine cellar, cobwebs and all (the man I bought it from was a wine dealer). I sketched the layout on the back of an envelope and had no idea how much of a life the place would take on with me. In the nearly 25 years since, it has seen me through marriage and divorce and motherhood. And it’s also grown, as I’ve been lucky to be able to buy the flat next door and the flat upstairs to make a few other small rooms. My daughter and our cockapoo, Eddie, now also call it home.

The whole story is in my new book, Returning Home, which comes out in January. This last renovation was the grown-up one, done properly with an architect, and even so, some of my favourite details came from having to sharpen my pencil. Rooms aren’t decorated with fabric and wallpaper alone; it’s all the stuff that makes the difference, and a lot of the best stuff is small. A beech pepper mill that actually works (and looks good left out on the counter). A tray by the bed for a cup of tea and a biscuit. Bud vases down the middle of the table, and a pair of snips that proved to be my gateway drug into gardening.

I have a terror of leaving scented candles burning, so I love the instant gratification and very non-burdensome quality of the room sprays by Perfumer H. It is like that spritz of fragrance you give yourself before leaving the house. I often use it just before friends arrive for dinner. Marmalade for winter is one of my favorites because I love the scent of bitter orange in the house.

This is the kitchen tool you didn’t know you needed — once you use it, you’ll never go back. I love to use fresh strawberries in desserts and have them for bites on trays when I entertain.

Every house needs books, the more the better. And one of my favorites is my good friend and collaborator Gil Schafer’s first book, The Great American House. Not only are the homes and photos beautiful, but the writing is too. It’s a perfect start for any library or coffee table.

I always tease my American friends about loving ice in their drinks, but really, is there anything more refreshing than an iced tea or lemonade out in the garden? These trays make huge cubes that don’t dilute your drink too quickly and look very chic in a glass.

I can never have too many trays, and neither can you. These from Colefax & Fowler are lovely and so useful for bedsides or using for a cup of tea and a biscuit.

[Editor’s note: The price is converted to USD from pounds.]

I love putting Maldon salt in pretty receptacles, and nice pepper mills can be quite hard to find. The David Mellor ones combine excellent mechanisms with beautiful design. The beech finish will be in style forever, and it’s worth splurging a little bit on things you use and touch every day.

You can’t have too many of these around your flat. I like them under the sink, in the laundry room, by the fireplace. The enamel is really smart and the soft brush is ideal for not scratching good floors.

Houses and Parties is one of my go-to sites, and it has converted me to the necessity of a cocktail napkin. These little napkins are such a nice thing to give a guest when they are holding a very icy, wet glass, and this set, with the charming appliqué mushrooms, definitely say “glamorous hostess.”

This chopping board is a staple in my kitchen, and it’s very clean looking, so I’m happy to leave it out. I love that it has a lip so it looks like a counter.

I love having bowls of these in my sitting room. It’s elegant (and indulgent) to have some really delicious, beautiful chocolates on display. But be warned: Get extras to have on hand because they taste delicious and are addictive.

These charming covers are a genius way to serve a canned drink. They look so pretty and they will save your furniture. A cold, wet can going down on the table can have tragic results.

I have a great supply of bud vases and decanters in my cupboard, and I love these magic copper balls for cleaning them. They’re perfect for a vase with a smaller opening and also keep harsh chemicals out of the vessel. No one wants to have bleach traces left when they are trying to get a flower arrangement to last.

I always go to KRB at the end of a project to accessorize, and I always get a handful of these terrific notepads. Historically, they were placed by the telephone. Now I put them beside beds and sofas with a pot of pencils nearby. I especially love “Complaints” and “Blah Blah Blah.”

These snips have been my gateway drug to gardening. Cutting flowers and deadheading with these beautiful things has definitely given me huge pleasure and joy, allowing me to spend time in my garden getting to know and understand my plants close up. It is amazing how, just doing that, my knowledge and confidence in gardening has grown.

These little jewels have gotten me out of jail several times when I have needed flowers in an instant. With very little, I have been able to create a cheerful arrangement with stems cut from my garden at the end of the season without much going on. They require very little in terms of flower arranging, so I find they are a trusty friend for tables, mantelpieces, and little trays on vanities.

entry.title: A Gift for Every Type of Sister
entry.summary: She may steal your clothes, but you’ll steal the favorite-sibling award.
entry.content:
As an older sibling, it’s virtually a requirement that I keep up with my younger sister’s changing tastes and opinions. And to prove just how well I know her, it’s essential that I go all out in the gift-giving department. That means choosing an item that’s surprising (as in, she wouldn’t think to buy it for herself) but touches on her interests or a recent memory of ours. With those qualifications in mind, I’ve gifted plenty of winners — for her birthday, important holidays we’ve spent apart, her college graduation, and her next big gig — that she can actually put to use while reminding her of our bond.

To help you find a gift that suits your sister, I’ve combed through our archives to uncover 45 standout ideas, many of which are Strategist-tested and -approved by a sister or were successfully gifted to one. And because no two sisters are exactly alike, I found delightful options for every type, including stylish sneakers that aren’t played out (as in, not Sambas) and something new for Owala-water-bottle loyalists.

Updated on October 27, 2026
These picks have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

If she needs help salvaging dry or frizzy hair, consider our favorite hair oil from Verb. It adds moisture to freshly washed hair and is suitable for all hair types (and not too heavy for fine hair).

Give her another series by fantasy romance author Sarah J. Maas to dive in to. House of Earth and Blood is the first book in The Crescent City series, which Maas’s publisher recommends reading after A Court of Thorns and Roses.

Whether she’s boarding a long-haul flight or relaxing after her nine-to-five, this soothing Biodance mask will brighten and soften her skin.

This foldable fan does double duty as a portable battery, so she can both stop complaining about the overactive radiator and stop “borrowing” your phone charger when you’re out.

We’ve been seeing this wavy mirrored phone case all over TikTok, and your perennially online sister will recognize it immediately.

These star-shaped pimple patches draw gunk out from active acne spots and are a handy way to prevent skin-picking. According to Paramore front woman Hayley Williams, they look cool on your face, too.

During the day, this charming mushroom-shaped nightlight will look like a toadstool sprouting from a wall, and at night, it’ll save your sister from turning on jarring overhead lights. It’s also color-changing for a little extra magic.

This four-piece set of Mario Badescu face mists will give her skin a dewy finish.

This faux-fur bucket hat feels straight out of a Delia’s catalogue. She can wear it through winter and into chilly spring days.

This weighted Hula-Hoop would make an excellent gift for a teen sister who’s still experimenting with movement because it’s a low-intensity workout she can do practically anywhere — even while watching TV. It was the only workout item mentioned multiple times when we surveyed teenagers about the (actually cool) stuff they’ve purchased.

These hypoallergenic earrings, made with 14-karat gold-plated sterling silver, are designed for everyday wear — and they’re under $20, if she ever needs to replace them.

If she finally gave gel extensions the boot, this tinted polish will repair her natural nails and give them a healthy-looking sheen. It contains hydrating and strengthening ingredients, such as vitamin E, calcium, and bamboo extract.

Owala’s Free Sip water bottle was super popular last year — in fact, no fewer than 11 Strategist staffers bought one. This fall, the brand launched a new product: a stainless-steel tumbler designed to hold hot or cold beverages and slim enough to fit into a car’s cup holder.

Give her the tea-sommelier-approved Yorkshire Gold that Sofia Coppola told us she drinks every morning.

Prepping for medical school is overwhelming (I know because my sister just started her first semester this fall). To lighten her mood, go for this coffee-table book, which has both scientific and witty descriptions of rare and common conditions.

This stretchy neoprene belt can fit your sister’s phone and keys. It’s tight enough to keep from bouncing when she’s running or on a quick (“hot girl”) walk. I own one and appreciate how comfortable it is to wear.

Instead of a traditional triangular martini glass, add this round-bottomed coupe to her bar cart. It’s easy to hold and offers a bit more heft, meaning less chance of spilling.

From the makers of the viral Five-Minute Journal, here’s a planner with guided prompts and inspirational quotes to encourage daily reflection and mindfulness.

We’ve been fans of Baleaf’s yoga pants for many years, and contributor Maggie Slepian says these outperform the pricier pairs from Alo, Prana, and Lululemon in her closet.

If your sister swears by the anti-aging power of retinol on her face, it might be time she tried body retinol. Naturium’s formula contains encapsulated retinol to improve skin texture and firmness, plus shea butter to target dryness.

We think this lap desk makes a great gift because it will let her recline anywhere while answering emails in (physical) comfort. It can easily fit a MacBook Air or Pro, plus it has a mouse pad, a phone stand, and a built-in ledge to keep her laptop from slipping.

Containing three types of salt sourced from New Zealand, the Himalayas, and Hawaii, this Osea body scrub is our top pick for dry skin. It makes even the tiniest apartment showers feel spa-like.

If she always goes for light, floral mocktails, gift her this spring-y nonalcoholic spirit that only needs a splash of tonic. Garden 108 has hints of hay, spearmint, rosemary, and thyme. It’s from the U.K.–based company Seedlip, a brand every expert mentioned when we asked them about everything you need to stock an alcohol-free bar.

She’ll appreciate these self-tanning drops that come recommended by Paris Hilton and give an Ibiza-like glow. Hilton says she uses the drops with a lotion, and the application lasts around a week.

This isn’t your average fitness mat. It’s designed to double as a block for exercises like tricep dips or push-ups, but it can also add a little extra support for at-home workouts.

If she’s mastered her folded French omelet, switch things up with this tamagoyaki pan for rolling eggs Japanese-style. This method creates a softer and more delicate texture that’s perfect for sandwiches or for serving sliced as a course in a DIY omakase.

She’ll finally stop rifling through her makeup bag with this compact vanity case that’s designed to organize cosmetics of every size. It comes with a removable insert to keep taller products like serums and foundations upright, which means there’s less chance of leakage.

This travel pillow may look like a padded scarf, but it feels like first class when she’s snoozing comfortably at 30,000 feet. When our writer Rachael Griffiths tested the Trtl on a 12-hour flight to Seoul, she was out like a light; it keeps your neck at a more natural and supportive angle, she says.

Unlike a pair of stepped-on tennis shoes, these puffy North Face mules have an elastic heel, making them ideal for slipping on when she’s running out to the bodega or taking her dog for a walk. I own a pair and love how cozy the outer PET material and fleece lining feel on frigid days.

Your sister likely knows that a good grinder is the key to better-tasting brews. She’ll be able to pour her favorite beans into this machine that has a powerful burr blade and 17 grind-size settings.

These retro sneakers have a low profile and are easy to pair with any outfit. They’re a favorite of contributor Mya Gelber, who tested ten pairs of sneakers to find everyday ones that are stylish, comfortable, and well-priced.

This fluffy bathrobe is among the best we’ve tested. It has a tie waist and pockets, and the material is highly absorbent, so she can go straight to lotioning up without needing another towel to wipe away leftover water.

These pajamas are a tried-and-true favorite at the Strategist; we’ve been recommending them since 2017. Part of what makes them excellent is that they never wrinkle, even if she’s been tossing and turning at night.

If she’s never experienced the thrill of easy slicing, get her this knife set, which includes all the basics plus kitchen scissors and six steak knives. The wood block will look attractive on her countertop and free up some much-needed drawer space.

If she’s moving out on her own after graduation, this air fryer will allow her to roast, bake, broil, and dehydrate meals for one (or many) in a snap. It has a touchscreen display and a dishwasher-safe basket for easy cleanup.

We know cleaning products are pretty unsexy, but this small (but mighty) Bissell will come in handy when it’s time to deep-clean her couch after another pet mess.

No matter where your sister takes the Sonos Roam — her living room or her favorite campground — its tuning technology automatically adapts to her surroundings, so the sound is always balanced. And because it supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, she can control it with just her voice.

For a super-active sister, this foot massager will work wonders on her cramps. It has three deep-kneading modes, five pressure settings, and a heat-therapy button to release tension and soothe achy arches ahead of race day (or just any day).

For about half the price of Dyson’s Airwrap, get her this multi-styling system from T3, which is the secret to my frizz-free blowouts. As someone with long, color-treated hair, I love how the blow-dryer attachment quickly dries my hair, and the ceramic curling barrels seal in shine.

I can’t say enough good things about this vibrating back wrap that eases muscle tension in my lower back and quickly decreases soreness. It has three different heat levels and three vibration patterns, plus it’s completely cord-free.

She’ll like this HigherDose mask, which uses red and near-infrared LEDs to target fine lines and wrinkles and stimulate collagen production. It’s made of high-quality silicone and has a cordless design that makes it great for multitasking or travel.

entry.title: A Gift for Every Type of Best Friend
entry.summary: From Kate McKinnon’s espresso-maker to a hangover-preventing probiotic drink.
entry.content:
Shopping for your best friend should be a walk in the park — you know them better than anyone — but finding a gift is never as easy as it seems. It’s impossible to fail in my best friend’s eyes, but that doesn’t stop me from (a) wanting to impress her and (b) giving her a present that conveys how much our friendship means to me. If you’re here shopping for a best friend, whether you’ve known each other since diapers or you just connected last year, I bet you feel the same.

So I’ve searched high and low to uncover 50 delightful gift ideas for any type of bestie. There’s a pair of elegant Sabre butter knives, the simple stovetop espresso-maker Kate McKinnon’s best friend introduced her to, and lots of other little things to make them smile. All these products are available on Amazon, and I’ve organized them by price so that you can easily find a present that fits both your best friend’s personality and your budget.

Updated on October 27, 2026
We still stand by these picks, which have been updated with the latest availability and pricing.

They’ll appreciate this lip-oil–stain hybrid, one of the brand’s newer products. It contains ceramides and peptides to lock in moisture and has buildable coverage.

While our beauty writer, Tembe Denton-Hurst, is a big fan of Dieux’s Instant Angel moisturizer — she says it’s nourishing and soothing without feeling heavy — the price tag is “painfully” steep. After she procrastinated on restocking it, Denton-Hurst turned to this moisturizer from CosRx. “It isn’t as lush feeling as the Dieux Instant Angel, but I’d argue it’s equally nourishing,” she writes.

Here’s a handbook by Ruoyi Jiang, the founder of Chop Suey Club, that breaks down the rules and explains the difference between traditional Chinese mahjong, American mahjong, and many other variations.

Whether they prefer their martinis bone dry or extra dirty, theirs will stay perfectly chilled thanks to the double-walled, vacuum-sealed stainless-steel design.

This scoop colander is one of the most-used tools in our senior editor Winnie Yang’s kitchen. Compared to a traditional colander, it’s more convenient for straining a single serving of udon or beans, retrieving boiled eggs, and rinsing berries under the tap, Yang says.

Owing to her husband’s seltzer obsession and the resulting recycling-bin overflow, Strategist contributor Leah Finnegan bought a can crusher. It works for containers that hold up to 16 ounces, from mini-cans to plastic water bottles, and “purports to reduce your recycling load by 20 percent, but I’d wager it’s even more,” Finnegan reports.

They’ll be able to organize work notes, medical records, and other documents with this notepad, which has 12 built-in folders. Eva Chen, who discovered this “during one of those Amazon middle-of-the-night wormholes,” loves that she doesn’t have to carry a notepad with her anymore.

At the other end of the spectrum is this mini 6.7-ounce water bottle, which our senior writer Liza Corsillo says is the “size of one glass of wine or one beach martini, and it’s an ideal amount of water for green juice or tea to have on hand for an average 35-minute subway ride.”

According to self-proclaimed “popcorn snob” Leah Finnegan, anyone who loves the snack will appreciate these thick kernels. They produce huge, fluffy popcorn pieces that can carry all kinds of seasonings.

A few years ago, our kitchen-and-dining writer Emma Wartzman received these metal line-makers as part of a care package from a friend. She now uses them exclusively to mark recipes in cookbooks.

A longtime top seller on our site, this silk pillowcase feels luxurious and helps to reduce frizz.

While the Halo cap is technically designed to target tension caused by headaches, it doubles as a sleep mask. Nikki Glaser has been using it for over a year and told us she buys it for all her friends who have trouble snoozing.

Your best friend can re-create a Korean bathhouse experience at home with these colorful mitts (beloved by Eva Mendes.) that exfoliate more precisely than loofahs, bathing cloths, or brushes.

This pill organizer — described as a “Mary Poppins Medicine Cabinet” for how much it can hold — would make a great gift for the best friend who always has Band-Aids on hand. The expandable carrier can also double as a travel case for jewelry.

If their dessert cravings hit hardest after lunch, these jelly-filled pouches are a satisfying (and relatively guilt-free) alternative to the office candy drawer. With a slurpable consistency that’s slightly chewy, the packable snack is available in flavors such as peach, mango, cola, and more.

If they complain about having to repurchase expensive skin-care products, get your best friend this rosacea-soothing serum, which contains the same peptides as Biologique Recherche’s $76 treatment. It has centella to target redness, glycerin to quench dehydration, and niacinamide to strengthen the skin’ barrier.

This kit of mood-boosting essential oils will help them reset after a long day. Juliette Lewis, who discovered the power of essential oils while working on set, says it’s “a very shortcut way to clear my head and refocus.”

John Derian told us he uses this olive oil for regular cooking — and we think it would make for an inexpensive (yet still thoughtful) gift.

If they aren’t able to visit C.O. Bigelow to buy one of Carolyn Bessette Kennedy’s tortoiseshell headbands, here’s an option that looks similar to CBK’s original (see here and here).

Lafco’s linen sachet is filled with resin beads that release a scent of gardenia, orange blossom, and ylang-ylang. Our junior writer, Bella Druckman, stashed one in her suitcase before a trip to Paris and says she was “honestly kind of blown away by the clean smell coming off my clothes.”

Handmade in France, Sabre’s set of bistro-style spreader knives is a thoughtful gift for your butter-loving bestie.

When our sleep writer, Amelia Jerden, tested six pairs of concert earplugs to find the best for hearing protection, the Earpeace earplugs won because of their comfort, customization options, sound clarity, and affordability. “They didn’t put much pressure on my ears, even after an extended period of time,” she says.

Strategist contributor Keren Lerner — who is not a doctor but a self-described “nutrition nerd” — purchased this kit and some seeds after learning that broccoli sprouts have 100 times higher levels of cancer-fighting phytochemicals than mature broccoli does. “We put them in smoothies for our kids, in salads (they add a nice radishlike flavor and good crunch), and on bread with peanut butter or hummus,” Lerner writes.

Kate McKinnon told us she uses this stovetop espresso machine, which her best friend (who is “obsessed with Italian things”) introduced to her. “There’s something about the tactile nature of it: just water, fire, and coffee beans ground to a fine powder and then, a minute later, there you are,” McKinnon says.

Corsillo loved the closeness this wrap-style baby carrier afforded her and her newborn son. “He was so comfortable and secure being held in the Boba that he usually fell asleep right away,” she writes.

These adorable Ralph Lauren socks are a step up from their basic gym socks. To complete the gift, pair them with our top-rated pajamas, which are available in sets with pants or with shorts for hot sleepers.

After a few too many dirty martinis, they’ll be glad they started the night with this pre-alcohol probiotic drink, which chef JJ Johnson swears by to curb hangovers. “I just left the Wine & Food Festival in South Beach. I took one every day I was there, and I wasn’t hungover,” Johnson says.

This Strategist-tested and -approved planner has light gridding on each page to jot down notes, write to-do lists, or even get some doodling in. Its hard-wearing cover will look just as good on December 31 as it did on January 1.

Plum Sykes says she received this bath oil from some friends, who had been gifted it by another friend. “I then give it to my friends. It’s become a bit of a cult. It’s always a hit, always,” she told us.

Comedian and actor Chelsea Handler swears by these sweet-tasting gummy bears for her daily intake of vitamins and minerals. “Sometimes I have them as dessert because rather than having something sweet and bad for you, I’m like, Well, these are good and good for you,” she says.

You probably know Yeti for its rugged performance coolers, but the brand’s wine chiller is also a winner. It can keep a one-liter bottle of white or rosé drinkably cool for hours on end. Our senior writer Michael Zhao says, unlike with an ice-pack sleeve, “I can place it directly onto a table without worrying about condensation ruining the wood or tablecloth beneath.”

This boxed set will take them through every wine region of France, featuring some 800 producers and more than 7,000 wines.

Here’s a leakproof set of magnetized containers that’ll make packing their travel-size liquids more organized (and less messy).

Help your best friend get back into reading with the five-book series that took over model Taylor Hill’s life (in a good way). “If I could go back and reread them again for the first time, that would make me so happy,” Hill says.

Eve Jobs credits her best friend with introducing her to Bala Bangles, which she now uses for leg, arm, and ab workouts. “They have their own little travel case, and I can do everything that I need with them,” Jobs says.

I’ve gifted this charming ring dish to a few of my close friends who are getting married this year. I love that it’s made from 100 percent recycled aluminum.

For sensitive noses, consider this clean-smelling scent from Lake & Skye that’s comparable to a fresh load of laundry. It even got Michelin-starred chef Missy Robbins to start wearing perfume.

They may have parted with their old air fryer, but the Ninja Crispi sets itself apart because it fries food in glass containers instead of the usual black Teflon-covered baskets. This plastic-free appliance converted our writer Arielle Avila into an air-fryer devotee: “Since getting the Ninja Crispi, I’ve used it at least three to four times a week. It’s almost replaced my oven and microwave altogether.”

Our tech writer Jordan McMahon says Hatch’s smart alarm clock fixed its biggest flaw by removing the need to keep your smartphone nearby to manage the device. Now you can toggle through wake-up and sleep routines, as well as turn on the bedside light, all right on the clock.

This red-light face wand helps reduce wrinkles, dark spots, and puffiness — and according to Strategist contributor Diksha Basu, who recently turned 40, it’s the secret to why her skin looks better now than it did in her 20s.

Marketing professional Tia Carson, who happens to be a West Village girl, put Caraway’s Dutch oven on her wish list. “Soup season has commenced, but now we need the right equipment,” Carson says.

Fellow is known for its stylish kettles and travel mug, and the brand’s latest coffee grinder is “​​more like a design object than my old Baratza,” says our writer Kat Gillespie. She uses hers for AeroPress or French press every morning and appreciates how easy the machine makes it to grind for a single cup.

With Cozy Earth’s sweaty-sleeper-approved pajamas, your best friend will finally stay cool (and dry) through the night. The moisture-wicking fabric is a big upgrade from the oversized cotton T-shirt they’ve been wearing to bed for years.

It’s pricey for a pepper mill, but professional chefs praise its heavy-duty construction and clever design that dispenses an “insane” volume of grinds with very little elbow grease.

I own and love this hand-finished dinnerware set from Vancouver-based Fable. It includes dinner plates, salad plates, and nicely sized breakfast bowls, so it will make a lovely housewarming gift for your friend who just moved away.

This sleek cannabis infuser is the perfect appliance for the budding home chef. The device infuses botanicals into oil and butter and also has drying and decarboxylation capabilities, which makes the process of cooking with cannabis or hemp much easier than what they tried to do in high school that one time.

entry.title: I’ll Be Buying My Leggings From Quince Now
entry.summary: Plus I found all-merino wool base layers and my new favorite work-from-home pants.
entry.content:
Over the past couple of years, we’ve tested all kinds of categories at Quince, from its puffer coats and bags to its bedding and kitchenware. I’ve personally reported on its summer dresses and wellness supplements. But as our resident fitness writer, I started to wonder why we haven’t tried best sellers from its activewear collection, which has plenty of practical-looking pieces that are cheaper alternatives to ones from brands like Lululemon, Alo Yoga, and Beyond Yoga. Some are even pretty close matches: The Ultra-Form Contour Jacket looks similar to Lululemon’s Define Jacket, and the Flowknit Wide Leg Pants remind me of Vuori’s Halo Essential Wideleg Pant. So I set out to try an assortment of Quince’s activewear and find out how the brand’s different fabrics hold up during actual workouts. Below, you’ll find high-rise leggings, merino-wool base layers, and the pants I haven’t wanted to take off for weeks.

This jacket basically inspired this story because I’ve purchased several of Lululemon’s waist-snatching Define Jackets over the years, which isn’t so great for my bank account. Quince’s Contour Jacket is 50 bucks, less than half the price of the Lululemon. They both have a sturdy center zipper and thumb holes at the cuff, which anchors the fabric and prevents the sleeves from shifting when I’m on a run or walk. As for the fabric, Quince’s Ultra-Form is very stretchy and buttery, and it seems technical enough that pilling wouldn’t be an issue. I was impressed with how flexible yet durable it felt during Pilates and slow-paced strength-style workouts. I picked a size S since I’m usually a 4 or 6 in Lululemon, and the fit was perfect for my broad shoulders.

I decided to try these leggings and the Power-Up bra below to match my Contour Jacket. As I mentioned, the Ultra-Form material has a performance feel that’s moisture-wicking and has antimicrobial properties. I picked the Ultra-Form leggings in my usual size S (I’m a size 4 in all my Lululemon leggings), and I do think I could have sized down to an XS since these were very high-waisted on my five-foot-five frame and I prefer a tighter legging. They were also a smidge loose in the waist (almost to the point of gapping). I decided to stick with the size S, and they’ve been my favorite for heated mat Pilates classes thanks to their weightless feel. I think I could also wear these on runs, but I might opt for the XS to make sure there’s no shifting.

Compared to Ultra-Form, Power-Up is a medium-to-high compression fabric, which worked well in the longline sports-bra silhouette I tested since it kept my chest secure. The thick straps and criss-cross back also provide nice support and lift, whether I’m doing a treadmill run or stretching my calves in a downward-facing dog.

The Ultra-Soft fabric is made for low-impact activities like yoga or Pilates, but it was also my favorite to lounge in. These are my pick if you’re looking for a pair of leggings you can comfortably wear all day, since they are plenty stretchy but also have a brushed, cottonlike softness. The extra-thick waistband stays in place nicely, doesn’t dig into my hips, and keeps everything sucked in. The V-Neck Cropped Tank is also incredibly comfortable. It doesn’t have cups, but I love wearing it under a sweater or hoodie, almost in place of a bralette.

Quince’s Flowknit reminded me of Vuori’s signature DreamKnit material, which is a staple in my closet (I own a number of DreamKnit joggers, cardigans, and more). The Quince fabric has a lightweight drape and solid breathability, but I don’t think it’s quite as buttery or sueded as the Vuori. Regardless, the wide-leg pants — which, might I add, are under $50 — have become my favorite work-from-home pants because I don’t feel like I have to be overly precious with them: I’ve cleaned my house while wearing them, I’ve snuggled up to my shedding (and slobbering) dogs, I’ve run errands in them, and I’ve even worn these wide-legs to bed a few times on chillier nights. The pull-on style has a drawstring waistband that makes them easy to adjust, and the only real drawback I see is the lack of pockets. Combined with the pullover crew, I feel much more put-together than when I’m wearing actual sweats around the house.

I’ve been wanting a lightweight and fast-drying all-merino-wool top for cool fall runs, and this more than met my expectations. The thickness is perfect for keeping my arms warm, and then it’s easy to shed the layer a few miles into my run as I heat up and tie the long-sleeve around my waist. For under $50, it’s a steal considering similar options from Smartwool and the North Face go for well over $100. Made with 100 percent Australian merino wool, I absolutely love that it doesn’t contain any plastics and it’s something I can wear during a range of workouts or even just daily errands. And because the fiber naturally resists bacteria and moisture buildup, it won’t hold onto odors like other gym clothes. The base-layer tee is next on my list.

The Satin-Sculpt fabric is newer and has the slickest texture of all the Quince activewear fabrics I tested. It has a cool-to-the-touch feel, and like the name says, there’s a clear satinlike sheen, which actually made them appear dressier when I first unboxed them. These also had the strongest compression of the pieces I tried; I would compare them to Alo’s sculpting Airlift leggings. I love compressive bottoms that offer a held-in sensation when I’m working out, so these were a big win. Again, I’m usually a size 4 in Lululemon leggings, so I went for a size S in these. At first, I was hesitant about the fit — I think a size XS could have worked for me, too — but it seems like these give me some wiggle room, which is nice in a legging with sturdier fabric. And with these being super high-rise, I’ll be interested to see if they hold their shape over time or begin to stretch out after more regular machine washes. So far, they’ve washed well — I hang-dry all of my exercise gear — and don’t roll down or budge during my lifting routine. On runs, there is some minor shifting due to the slipperiness of the material, but nothing too major.

entry.summary: Picks for every type of wife at every price point.
entry.content:
The closer the relationship you have with someone, the more pressure there is to find the right gift. So, if you’re shopping for your wife, I imagine you’re sweating. Whether you’re a newlywed trying to nail it, someone trying to say “I love you as co-parent but also as a person,” or a pair who’s been gifting for so long you’ve resorted to really scraping the barrel, it seemingly never gets easier. That’s why I’m here to help.

I’ve combed the Strategist archives, rummaged through my mental Rolodex, and also interviewed many tasteful, stylish wives in order to put together a list of gift ideas. I’ve covered a lot of bases here, so all manner of wives (from those in marathon training to wives who have a tinned-fish obsession) are catered to. My forever gifting philosophy is to mix highbrow and lowbrow. Stuff a Coach bag full of her favorite childhood candy! Get her a fancy stand mixer to go along with a new cookbook! Or perhaps some absurdly luxurious pajamas to pair with a restock of fluffy socks. You know her the best!

Just a couple spritzes on the bottom of her feet should help her get a good night’s rest, according to Strategist contributor Diksha Basu.

I’m not paying that much for a mushroom.’ Then they give you some so you’re like, ‘Oh, that shit is good.’ That’s what this does, in a cheaper version.”

The Advent-calendar elves are working overtime this holiday season. There are more than quadruple the number of Advent calendars in this roundup compared with last year.
