If you’re looking for more of our (early) holiday coverage, we have definitive guides to the best early beauty Advent calendars, Advent calendars for Gen Z, food Advent calendars, and Advent calendars for kids this year.

Update on October 27, 2026
﻿I added more Advent calendars, including from Kiehl’s and Fishwife, removed those now sold out, and checked the price and availability of all the others here.

You’re getting deluxe samples of EltaMD’s UV Clear Blemish-Prone & Oil Balancing SPF 50 and SkinMedica HA5 Hydra Collagen Water Burst Moisturizer, a full-size iS Clinical GeneXC Serum, and a trial-size Barbara Sturm Face Cream (which starts at $75 for 20mL).

Ulta calls this year’s 25 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar its “biggest Advent calendar yet.” You’ll unbox a Tatcha Rice Wash, Moroccanoil’s Moroccanoil Treatment, Osea Malibu Undaria Algae Body Oil, and about-face Fractal Glitter Eye Paint.

Take it from me, a former Anthropologie employee: The company’s beauty Advent calendars sell out faster than you can say “Maeve.” This year’s Beauty Advent Calendars — in 24- and 12-day versions — are already sold out (for now). But Anthropologie’s Holiday in the City is still available. It’s a whiff of the holiday sprit with festive-scented candles — snowmint, mistletoe and moss, cranberry fizz, sugar plum and vanilla woods, and evergreen and embers — and a juniper-cedar room spray.

When senior writer Dominique Pariso sniffed her way through drugstore candles, Voluspa’s came out as the fanciest. In this selection of the brand’s votives is French Cade Lavender (a woodsy lavender that reminds Pariso of her grandfather’s aftershave), Goji Tarocco Orange, Moso Bamboo, Crushed Candy Cane, Foraged Wildberry, and Noble Fir Garland.

Pariso called Yankee Candle “the best bang for your buck” of the drugstore candles. Burn through classic Yankee Candle scents — Midsummer’s Night, Lemon Lavender, Christmas Cookie, and Macintosh — with this calendar. Compared with the standard Yankee Candle that’s 22 ounces, every Yankee Candle here is 1.3 ounces.

A tribute to “the home of the bath bomb,” the 29½ High Street Advent Calendar features “bath treats” available only during the holidays (Sugar Plum Fairy, candy cane, reindeer) and six exclusives (including a carrot bath bomb and a mini swirly sticky-dates bubble, plus other Lush customer favorites like Unicorn Horn, Luna’s Butterfly, and Sleepy).

Just like the 29½ High Street Advent Calendar, this includes products available only during the holidays (such as a s’mores shower gel and hot-chocolate and orange lip scrub) and ten “gift-exclusive treats” (Turmeric Latte Dusting Powder, Santa’s Favorite Body Spray, Golden Bear Bath Bomb). But you can keep the pamper hamper itself well after Christmas, as the copy says.

Our Gen Z correspondent Bella Druckman says in her guide to the best Advent calendars for Gen Z that “Urban Outfitters’ calendar may as well have been designed by a high-schooler,” as it includes Starface pimple patches and a Billie Eilish perfume on the top of teens’ wish lists last year.

Another year, another 25 Day Advent Calendar from Revolve. 2026’s assortment may be the best yet, with a full-size Summer Fridays Dream Lip Oil, Foreo Mini UFO Device (and a Call It a Night Mask pack), and Tarte Tartelette Tubing XL Mascara. And the minis aren’t bad either — with a Sol De Janeiro Bum Bum oil, Ouai detox shampoo, and Tower 28 SOS Daily Rescue spray among them.

[Editor’s note: This is available for preorder now and estimated to ship between October 31 and November 10.] 

Not to be outdone, the 12 Days of Revolve — which, at $89, is one of the most affordable Advent calendars here — is back with a full-size Kosas Lip Pulse and Ilia Limitless Lash Mascara, plus a mini-size Summer Fridays Cloud Dew Moisturizer and Allies of Skin GF Serum.

Deluxe, “travel-ready” versions of Sunday Riley’s dermatologist-approved Good Genes and Beauty Hall of Famer C.E.O. vitamin C serum arrive inside the carry-on–themed 12 Days of Skincare.

Featuring Laneige’s Lip Sleeping Mask, which Yuna Zarai, Ty Hunter, Ashley Benson, and Keke Palmer can’t live without — alongside the company’s Water Sleeping Mask and Lip Glowy Balm.

Korres’s Greek Yoghurt Wide Awake Eye Gel keeps me from looking tired, and I’m happy to see it included here with the “best of 30 years of Korres,” like its Santorini grape body milk, basil-lemon shower gel, and mandarin-neroli hand cream. True to the brand’s heritage, the 24 boxes the products come in are decorated with a symbolic tama.

Everyone from Buzz Bissinger to contributor Hannah Goldfield swears by L’Occitane. Some of its classics — the almond shower oil that helps keep Denton-Hurst’s legs looking freshly lotioned and shea-butter hand cream — are in the Prestige Advent Calendar.

The ultimate Manicurist manicure — with nail polishes, a corrector pen, a base coat, a top coat, a cuticle remover, buffer, and a file (a total of 24 full-size products) — right at your fingertips.

Open three full-size products, three travel sizes, and 18 minis in Kiehl’s 24 Days of Joy — including a Midnight Recovery Concentrate that “works like a magic eraser overnight“; Creme de Corps, which Rachel Antonoff moisturizes with; and Ultra Facial Barrier–Hydrating Cleanser that keeps associate editor Jeremy Rellosa’s skin feeling refreshed.

At Beekman 1802’s Kindness Cafe, a barista goat carrying pastries and coffee leads you to a mint and eucalyptus whipped body lotion, pistachio-dark cherry hand cream, and honey and orange blossom soap.

For the Ruby Woo wearer, 24 Days of M.A.C Icons offers lipsticks, lip pencils, and eye shadows in the brand’s best-selling shades, including Spice and Oh, Baby.

“Every jewel-handled drawer” of Charlotte Tillbury’s Beauty Treasure Chest has either a full-size (six in all) or travel-size Charlotte Tilbury product — from the Airbrush Flawless setting spray in updates coordinator Najwa Jamal’s makeup bag to a Pillow Talk lipstick.

Modeled after Jo Malone’s London townhouse, it has the brand’s signatures — English pear and sweet pea, lime basil and mandarin, and wood sage and sea salt — in cologne, hand-cream, and body-cream forms.

Seasonal Jo Malone favorites like ginger biscuit, myrrh and tonka, and orange bitters, which “smells like a pomander — festive in a Victorian way, not a Hallmark way,” says our senior editor Ailbhe Malone, are in this year’s calendar. And on the 25th day, there’s a 30-ml.-size fragrance (tangerine and honey) — for comparison, the other samples are 9 ml., while a full-size is 100 ml.

In “an enchanted forest imagined with the artist Jean-Simon Roch,” Diptyque’s Feu de Bois, Baies, Orphéon, Sapin, and Rhubarbe reside.

Try an Augustinus Bader formula every day of the 12 Days of Bader. Maybe the Cream, which former Cut beauty director Kathleen Hou referred to as “the secret to rich-person skin,” or the Vitamin C Serum (our editor Lauren Levy noticed her skin was more even-toned after using it for a few weeks) will become a permanent step in your routine.

Coming in at a whopping $955 — the most expensive Advent calendar on our list (so far) — this has a combination of familiar Byredo scents like Mojave Ghost and Bibliothèque, with makeup (a Rouge à Lèvres in Liquide Vinyl Fantôme and Satin Earth Dust) and “objects for everyday use,” including a candle-wick trimmer and pocket mirror.

You don’t have to wait for the next day to open these Bonne Maman jams (including limited-edition caramel with salted butter, strawberry with Madagascar vanilla, and raspberry with dark chocolate), as our senior editor Jen Trolio’s family opens theirs in a single go to enjoy with her husband’s homemade bread.

It’s the perfect surprise for a chocolate lover: creations of milk, dark, and white chocolate with other flavors such as caramel, raspberry, passion fruit, praline, coconut, and even birthday cake.

The 25 original confections inside Dandelion’s calendar are made by 24 confectioners (who were chosen after a series of blind tastings). Each chocolate comes in an ornament box with Danish artist Lisa Grue’s illustrations, and there’s a storybook of Nordic folklore and a star decoration for your window (a Scandinavian tradition) included.

[Editor’s note: This is available on preorder now and estimated to ship in November.] 

In Compartés’s “whimsical kingdom” — where there’s a dragon and a castle beyond snowy pines — there are chocolates in flavors of buttered croissant, eggnog crème brûlée, pistachio marzipan, and salted honeycomb behind every door.

[Editor’s note: This is available on preorder now and estimated to ship on November 2.]

There’s no place like the Vermont Country Store, where you can get these liqueur-filled chocolates with Rhum St. James, Gin Gibson, Poire Williams, Kirsch Cherry, and Cognac Bayet from Abtey.

Charbonnel et Walker was granted a royal warrant under Queen Elizabeth II in 1970 (other customers were Princess Margaret, Lauren Bacall, and Noël Coward). This year’s calendar, inspired by the brand’s Bond Street store, is filled with truffles in flavors like sea-salt praline, white chocolate with strawberry conserve, and milk chocolate with hazelnut cream.

Bissinger’s has been in the confectionery business since 1668. “Inspired by the heritage of the Bissinger’s boutique,” this year’s Advent calendar has a glaceed orange au chocolat and dark bouche de noel truffles.

Once upon a time, Tony’s Chocolonely was the next status Halloween candy. It has remained a Strategist favorite over the years. In the brand’s Countdown Calendar, you get an assortment of chocolates with nougat, caramel, and hazelnut.

Chef Jonathan Waxman admits “Walker’s are better than any [shortbread] I could make.” (He learned how to make shortbread from a Joy of Cooking recipe.) The individually wrapped biscuits in Walker’s calendar include all-butter fingers (Waxman says, “If you dip them in chocolate, it’s not such a bad thing”) and salted-caramel squares.

This house includes 24 German lebkuchen (often compared to gingerbread): chocolate-orange stars, milk chocolate with a sour-cherry filling, and pfeffernuse.

Filled with traditional kekserln like sacher husarenkrapferl (a chocolate-covered almond-vanilla thumbprint cookie with apricot jam), it may be the closest thing to the Café Sabarsky reopening.

Enjoy Ladurée confections like chocolate Eugenié biscuits, hazelnut-vanilla pearls, and langues de chat in this year’s Advent calendar. And the first 140 customers to preorder will receive marshmallow bears — one in milk chocolate and the other dark chocolate — as a special treat.

[Editor’s note: This is available for preorder from October 1 to October 31, with delivery in November.]

A Marriott collaboration with Laila Gohar (and illustrations by Joana Avillez) features Casa Bosques chocolates inspired by resort locations, such as almonds and Meyer lemons for San Francisco, and pistachios and raspberries for Munich.

Maybe an upgrade to Swedish fish are these gummies in strawberry-pomegranate, strawberry-apple, melon, and watermelon.

Nearly every “candy food group” is represented in the 24 Days of Sweets by Dylan’s Candy Bar, including jelly rings, milk chocolate, and cotton candy.

Following the Swedish tradition of lördagsgodis, there are extra-generous-size surprises on the Saturdays of Sockerbit’s candy Advent calendar.

In the immortal words of Scary, Sporty, Posh, Baby, and Ginger Spices: “Spice up your life.” You could do so with the help of Parisian spice distributor Le Comptoir Colonial’s Spice Advent Calendar for Williams Sonoma, with za’atar (thyme, sumac, sesame), paella seasoning (paprika, turmeric, caraway), and speculoos blend (cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, anise, ginger) included.

Williams Sonoma’s 12 Days of Cheese is for those who understand the nuances of Muenster and cheddar (or just Kraft singles). Each cheese is made by a family-operated creamery in Utah from the milk of a fourth-generation dairy and other ingredients like wildflower honey, organic bergamot, and cayenne pepper.

A real popcorn snob needs kernels of purple, red, and sweet baby blue and seasonings of dill pickle, white cheddar, and buttery jalapeño from “Indiana’s popcorn country.”

Only the finest ingredients for the home cook: a Sutter Buttes balsamic vinegar and wildflower honey, Jacobsen sea salt, Nielsen-Massey and Madagascar bourbon vanilla extract, with a Williams Sonoma dark-chocolate peppermint bark and brown-sugar bear.

All the best snacks Harry & David offers: a Royal Riviera pear, Moose Munch popcorn, Mesa Verde trail mix, and Scharffen Berger chocolate squares.

If you (tastefully) eat fish from a can, here’s Fishwife’s smoked Alaskan sockeye with Spanish extra-virgin olive oil, sardines with preserved lemon, and mussels with sweet pepper and chile.

Fly by Jing’s 12-day Advent calendar returns this year with more unlaunched sauces and discontinued blends. (It sold out on November 5 last year, according to the brand — you know what to do.)

After tasting Whittard’s hot chocolate in London, I can’t go back to Swiss Miss. Try the company’s salted caramel, sticky toffee pudding, and cinnamon roll hot flavors for yourself with its Hot Chocolate Advent Calendar. There are two single-serve sachets in the drawers — if you’re willing to share.

Or tea drinkers might appreciate Whittard’s Loose Leaf Advent Calendar instead, with lapsang souchong, silver needle, English rose, and jasmine dragon pearls to sip.

In the Palais des Thés’s constellation-filled sky are the Parisian company’s Grand Yunnan Impérial black tea, Genmaicha Yama green tea, and L’Herboriste N°52 infusion (with peppermint, anise, and lemon balm), plus other blends and herbal infusions.

Maybe Red Bull’s juneberry, Fuji apple and ginger, and white peach flavors will give you wings.

Sample varietals — rosé, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc — from Total Wine’s Winery Direct line.

Stationery nerds: Papier’s 24-day Advent calendar and first-ever 12-day Advent calendar are here with roller-ball pens, fine liners, and highlighters for pen freaks and thank-you cards and sticky tabs for those who still hand-write everything.

Or there’s a separate Anthropologie and Papier collaboration with a shopping-list notepad, pencil case, and A7 notebooks.

The lack of a reference image means you may need all the help you can get to solve this “puzzling experience” from Nautilus. (It was part of a new guard of non-fusty puzzles in a market dominated by the likes of Ravensburger and Springbok.) Per instructions: The first 12 drawers contain between 40 and 56 pieces, while the 13th box has 106 pieces to complete the rest of the puzzle (for a total of 688 pieces).

Whether you’re still figuring out your color-analysis chart or rereading Sanzo Wada’s A Dictionary of Color Combinations, you may find inspiration for your new wall paint in Pantone’s 24 Days of Colorful Pop-Out Ornaments. Every day includes a Pantone color chip attached to a cord to be hung on a Christmas tree or strung together in a garland.

Read a miniature hardback title from Charles Dickens, L.M. Montgomery, Louisa May Alcott, and Hans Christian Andersen as a bedtime tradition in the days before Christmas. Just be sure to have your readers nearby.

Here are 25 rubber ducks costumed as a witch, a knight, a fireman, and even a golf ball for a bather or Jeep owner (hat tip to our writer Amelia Jerden).

Consider gifting Swedish Stockings’ hosiery instead of more socks. This set has a pair of Svea Tights in 30 denier and Ines Shimmery Socks in both black and bordeaux.

The new movie-themed LEGO Advent calendar designs are of Disney Princesses Ariel, Cinderella, Moana, and Mulan; Star Wars “featuring the Mandalorian in an ugly Christmas sweater”; and a Marvel scene with Spider-Man on skis, says our resident toy expert Liza Corsillo.

LEGO’s 2026 Friends Advent calendar has Nova, Liann, and Aliya writing to Santa with the help of animal friends like a seal, polar bear, and penguin.

Maisonette’s boys’ 25 Days of Holiday Surprises features toy cars and make-believe accessories, while its girls’ 25 Days of Holiday Surprises has jewelry and arts and crafts.

For the kid with a need for speed, here are ten 1:64 scale Hot Wheels vehicles (a snow globe car with a Yeti driver among them) to have a Fast & Furious–style race.

Meet the residents of Busytown — Hilda Hippo, Huckle Cat, Sally Cat, and Mr. Frumble — with each pop-out ornament in Richard Scarry’s Best Advent Calendar Ever. Included is a 150-inch gold cord to make a garland.

The burgeoning geologist will like opening specimens of agate, aventurine, hematite, sodalite, and tiger’s eye every day of National Geographic’s gemstone calendar. And there’s a dig brick of rose quartz for the grand finale.

Under each pocket is a new sticker sheet of Dick Bruna’s storybook bunny. Keep the beribboned trifold portfolio (which resembles Miffy’s house) on a wall, desk, or mantle.

Billed as “the ultimate festive Where’s Waldo?,” it includes 24 search-and-find mini-books of the bespectacled character (who’s known as Wally elsewhere). And there’s a press-out of Waldo on Christmas Day to hide as you wish (maybe not by an Elf on the Shelf).

A collaboration between Meri Meri and the New York City Ballet, this is based on a production of George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker and features a charm bracelet on the first day and themed charms (like a ballerina in a tutu and lollipop) to go on it the next days.

Your kid can do their own manicure using Olive & June’s 12 Days of Mani Magic with Pressies and nail-art stickers.

Imagine giving Samantha Parkington a cell phone, Josefina Montoya a pair of sunglasses, or Felicity Merriman a faux-fur scrunchie — or any of the other American Girl doll accessories in the Surprises 2026 Advent Calendar.

entry.title: The 11 Very Best Sound Machines
entry.summary: Including mechanical, electronic, portable, sound-machine–alarm-clock combos, and tinnitus-friendly options.
entry.content:
Whether you’re trying to mask the noise around you or fill the silence, a sound machine can be a handy sleep aid. The constant background noise it creates can drown out loud (potentially sleep-disrupting) noises, foster relaxation, and create a sense of comfort and familiarity, according to neuropsychologist Dr. Sanam Hafeez. But a good sound machine doesn’t just make sound — it should also be easy to use, provide appealing sound options, and potentially even be aesthetically pleasing. To find sound machines that fit the bill, I talked to Hafeez, as well as a sleep researcher, about how sound machines impact sleep, spoke to sound-machine users (some of whom feel very passionately about their sound-machine preferences), and called in a few options to test myself.

Below, you’ll find sound machines offering a variety of sound types as well as machines in various shapes and sizes to match different needs and design preferences. If you’d rather block out the noise altogether, take a look at our guide to the best earplugs for sleeping. Or if you’re shopping for kids, check out our favorite sound machines for babies.

Updated on October 27, 2026
I added two new sound machines: a two-in-one white-noise machine and fan, and a two-in-one portable white-noise machine and Bluetooth speaker. I also confirmed pricing and availability for all the sound machines we recommend.

The two main types of sound are mechanical and electronic. A mechanical sound machine uses a physical mechanism to make noise — usually a fanlike device that creates a whirring sound. An electronic sound machine, on the other hand, plays an audio recording of a sound. Neither is better than the other; it mostly comes down to personal preference. With a mechanical sound machine, you will likely have only one sound type, which you may be able to slightly adjust. With an electronic sound machine, you are likely to have at least a few different sound options to choose from and will likely have more volume control.

Mechanical sound machines primarily make the kind of ambient noise colloquially referred to as “white noise,” though it may or may not be actual white noise. Technically, white noise refers to a sound “that covers the entire range of audible frequencies, all of which possess equal intensity,” according to the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hafeez says that because white noise merges all sound frequencies, it is effective for drowning out environmental sounds that could affect sleep. Chiropractor and sleep researcher Dr. Robert Oexman notes that white noise may be particularly helpful for shift workers who sleep in the daytime, people with tinnitus, or those who need help calming a “busy brain.” There are other types of ambient sound named for colors, with pink and brown noise being used most commonly in sound machines designed for use while sleeping. Electronic sound machines may also produce white, pink, or brown noise via a recording of the sound.

Unlike mechanical sound machines, electronic ones can also have a host of other sound types, including ocean waves, rainfall, birds chirping, or even music. Hafeez says that nature sounds can trigger a relaxation response in the brain, both because they create a serene atmosphere and because they “typically follow predictable, rhythmic patterns, which help lower heart rates and ease anxiety, facilitating easier sleep onset.”

Some sound machines have an internal rechargeable battery or will run on batteries. That makes them much more travel-friendly or convenient to move to different spaces throughout your home. I’ve indicated whether each machine below needs batteries, is rechargeable, or whether it needs to be plugged into an AC and/or USB power source.

I’ve listed the approximate dimensions of each sound machine, so you know if it will fit where you intend to use it or will be convenient for travel.

Where relevant, I’ve noted any important features that help or hinder using the device.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 10 fan sounds, 10 white/pink/brown noise sounds, and 2 ocean surf sounds | Power source: AC or USB | Size: 4.7” x 4.7” x 3.3” | Notable features: Physical buttons on top of the machine

The LectroFan Evo earned the top spot on this list for an electronic sound machine because it strikes a nice balance between being versatile and being easy to use. It comes highly recommended by multiple Strategist staffers who are quite choosy about their sound machines, and after testing it myself, I have to agree it earns its crown. While there are sound machines with more features out there, I think the LectroFan offers a good amount of customization without veering into overcomplication. It is also one of the loudest sound machines I’ve tested and has some of the best audio quality I’ve heard from an electronic sound machine. Even when I’ve fully cranked up the volume, the audio sounds crisp and clear.

Strategist writer Lauren Ro and senior editor Jen Trolio have each tried both the LectroFan and the Yogasleep Dohm (our pick for best mechanical sound machine, below) and prefer the LectroFan overall. Ro likes the variety of pitches you can choose from on the LectroFan; Trolio adds that the LectroFan getting much louder than the Dohm is another reason it won out for her.  

The LectroFan is fairly small, so it doesn’t take up much space on a nightstand (it’s also a good deal smaller than the Dohm). Ro even takes hers along when she travels. It has physical buttons on top of the machine — there’s no need to use an app or consult a manual to use it — as well as a sleep timer. While it has to be plugged in, you can use either a USB port or an AC outlet, and it comes with an adapter.

One downside to the simple controls of the LectroFan is that you have to cycle through the sound selections to find the one you want, so if you accidentally hit that button (while fumbling around in the dark, for example), you’ll have to go through all the sounds to return to your original setting.

Sound type and variety: Mechanical noise, adjustable volume | Power source: AC | Size: 5.5” x 5.5” x 4” | Notable features: 7-foot power cable, single on-off switch

The Yogasleep Dohm uses an internal fan to generate a “white noise” sound mechanically. The simple device has been around since 1962 and has gained many fans along the way, including Emma Roberts, politician Andrew Yang, and several Strategist staffers. I even recently spotted several Dohms strategically placed around my therapist’s office to mask sound from room to room.

The fan runs at two speeds, and there are two different pieces you can twist to alter the sound and adjust the volume — one that opens or closes holes on top of the machine, and one that opens and closes holes along the sides. Manipulating one or both of them allows air to escape the device differently, raising or lowering the volume and resulting in tones that subtly range between a “lighter, airier” sound or a lower hum. It is exceptionally easy to use — even though you can twist the case to change the volume and get a slightly different sound, you really just have to plug it in and switch it on, so it’s very appealing for those who hate futzing. One such user is Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang, who prefers the Dohm over the LectroFan because “the switch has a really nice, satisfying heavy click when you flip it, and the twist adjustment is intuitive and simple.” That keeps her from hitting the wrong button and accidentally changing settings, as she’s done with the LectroFan, which forces her to cycle back through all the options to find the right one. “As someone who has used these primarily for babies and toddlers, and is therefore usually sleep-deprived and time-crunched, it’s very appealing to have so few options with the Dohm,” Yang adds.

With electronic sound machines, there’s always a possibility of the sound feeling too artificial, or even the track noticeably looping. The Dohm sounds like a fan but without the air current a fan makes. After comparing the Dohm head-to-head with the LectroFan Evo, above, I decided I prefer the Dohm’s “acoustic” white noise (as my partner called it) over the recordings on the LectroFan. Senior editor Simone Kitchens is also on Team Dohm because she likes the “real” whirring sound of the Dohm over electronic white noise, and doesn’t have to choose which “type” of white noise to listen to. However, there is a limit on how loud the Dohm can get: Even when I turned it to its highest setting and twisted the cap to allow as much sound to escape as possible, the Dohm did not get nearly as loud as an electronic sound machine could.

Another con for the Dohm is that it can only be plugged into an AC power outlet. But it does have a seven-foot-long power cord, which makes it a little easier to use if your outlets are inconveniently spaced. And finally, in the white/gray colorway I tested, I think it looks a little like a medical device, though it also comes in white/pink, white/green, white/blue, and charcoal. Or for more color options, consider the Dohm Classic, which has the same internal mechanics as the version I tested but an older exterior design. It, too, is available in a sterile-looking white, as well as pink, tan, gray, and black.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 15 sounds, including white noise, various nature sounds, and three lullabies | Power source: AC | Size: 4” x 4” x 6.6” | Notable features: App-controlled, various light options, and optional Hatch+ subscription ($4.99 per month)

The Hatch Baby is the newest version of our favorite baby sound machine, previously called the Hatch Rest. We’ve received plenty of glowing recommendations for the Rest, and the Hatch Baby has an updated design and new features. It can also function as a nightlight or sunrise alarm clock, and with an optional Hatch+ subscription, which costs $70 per year or $7 per month after a three-month free trial, you’ll get access to a library of lullabies, bedtime stories, and guided meditations — though there is also a selection of free sounds. As with other Hatch products, it’s fun to play around with because there are so many customization options: You can choose from a wide range of colors to create a vibey feel for a bedtime wind-down routine as well as establish a light and “okay to wake” schedule. Everything is controllable through the corresponding smartphone app, but one big button on top of the device can quick-start your designated sound and adjust the volume.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 16 sound options, including 7 nature sounds, 3 white noise sounds, 3 fan sounds, and 3 lullabies | Power source: Rechargeable battery; comes with a USB-C charging cord | Size: 1.8” x 1.8” x 1.9” | Notable features: Comes with optional strap, physical buttons on underside

This sound machine is one of the smallest I have ever seen — it’s about the size of an egg, and I can almost wrap my hand around it. With 16 sound options, volume controls, and sleep timer options (30, 60, or 90 minutes), it does much of what a larger sound machine does, but takes up only a fraction of the space. I also appreciate that it comes with an optional strap, which allows you to hang it or attach it to a bag strap or key ring. And because it runs on rechargeable batteries, you can truly use this little machine anywhere.

If you’re picky about sounds, however, the Restnature may not be for you. Some of the sounds have a slightly canned quality, and I found that the rainfall and fire-crackling options also had some white-noise fuzz in the background. Overall, it sounds a little less crisp than the LectroFan and Hatch Rest.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 11 sound options, including 5 fan sounds, 4 white-noise sounds, and 2 ocean-surf sounds | Power source: Rechargeable battery; comes with a USB-C charging cord | Size: 2” x 2” x 2”, about 3.25 inches when speaker is swiveled up | Notable features: Can be used as a microphone or Bluetooth speaker, and multiple devices can be used for stereo sound

This is the portable sound machine Trolio regularly travels with — most recently, she used it during a Girl Scouts camping weekend to sleep soundly in a cabin she shared with a dozen 10- and 11-year-olds and their mothers. It conveniently recharges via USB-C so she can use the same cord she brings for her iPhone, and the top swivels up so she can direct the sound toward her or away from her. It also gets quite loud for its small size, and, as a bonus, can be used as a Bluetooth speaker for playing music or a microphone/speakerphone for calls.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 10 sound options, including white noise, ocean, and fan | Power source: USB-C power and rechargeable battery | Size: 6” x 2.76” x 2.17” | Notable features: Hanging clip

Hatch also makes an excellent portable option for kids on the go. It’s vaguely orb-like with an attached clip that makes it easy to hang on a stroller, diaper bag, or car seat like a key chain. (Though, notably, my top pick for a general-use portable sound machine, above, is smaller!) It’s beloved by Poppylist co-founder Tamiz Ahmed and family practitioner Dr. Laura Purdy for its ability to mask sound, even in noisy environments. Despite its size, they say the volume goes quite high. The Hatch Go is rechargeable and has a 15-hour battery life — it takes about two hours to fully recharge. It’s particularly nice-looking and comes in five colors (mint, peach, putty, honey, and slate), and the outer shell is made from post-consumer recycled plastic.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 3 white-noise sound options | Power source: USB power and rechargeable battery | Size:  3.4” x 1.6” x 3.84” | Notable features: Flexible hanging clip and nightlight

For another kid-specific portable option, senior editor Ailbhe Malone recommends this Hushh model by Yogasleep (the maker of our best mechanical sound machine, the Dohm). “We’ve used it in Airbnbs, hotels, and guest rooms to mask a cacophony of noises,” Malone says, noting that while there are only three noise variations, her 1-year-old daughter likes the general white-noise setting the most. New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff has also tried this sound machine and likes that it’s “extremely lightweight.” Similar to the Hatch Rest Go, there’s a carabiner on the machine to clip it to a stroller, car seat, or travel crib.

The overall size of the Hushh is similar to the Hatch Rest Go, but the Hushh is more pancake-shaped, while the Hatch is more spherical. For Malone, the Hushh is small enough to simply toss in her purse. The battery on the Hushh is designed to last up to eight hours, though Malone says hers doesn’t always last all night if left unplugged. It can be plugged in but is also easily rechargeable via USB to bring on the go. Other features include a small nightlight function (though it’s not enough to illuminate a room) and a child-lock function that will help prevent a curious toddler from turning it on or off. If you don’t care about the nightlight or the child lock, I also tried Yogalseep’s non-baby-specific portable sound machine called the Rohm, which is about $10 cheaper and doesn’t have those two features. It also has a tie-able lanyard instead of a clip but is otherwise is very similar.

Sound type and variety: Electronic; 6 sound options, including moving water, soft piano, Tibetan meditation music | Power source: Rechargeable battery, comes with a micro-USB charging cord | Size: 2.4” x 2.4” x 3.2” | Notable features: Physical buttons on the back

What made this Pure Enrichment sound machine stand out to me compared to the others I tested were the sounds it offered. I turned it on to test and immediately felt transported from my bedroom to a day spa or yoga studio. The options are much more musical than those of most of the other machines on this list; one sounds like meditation singing bowls, another like musical wind chimes, and still another like a contemplative synth. For those who prefer something other than straight white noise or basic nature sounds, it’s a great option.

The machine is also quite small and reasonably portable — about the same size as the Hatch Rest Go — though it’s still larger than the Restnature Mini. It has a rechargeable battery and relatively basic button controls on the back, which allow you to rotate through the six sound options, set a sleep timer (for ten, 30, or 60 minutes), and control the volume. It’s also noticeably more aesthetically pleasing than similar machines.

Sound type and variety: Electronic, 100+ sound options, including ambient noise and meditation tracks; Bluetooth-enabled | Power source: AC power and back-up battery, comes with USB-C cord and adapter| Size:  6.5” x 2.75” x 2.75” | Notable features: Alarm clock, nightlight, Bluetooth connectivity, optional app control

If you want to combine your sound machine and alarm clock into one, the Loftie is a sleek and simple option. While the Loftie is first and foremost an alarm clock, it has a vast library of audio options that make it a great choice for a sound machine too. Strategist writer Jeremy Rellosa loves his Loftie alarm clock and regularly uses the sound options to fall asleep at night. He says the sound options are high-quality, both in terms of the content and audio itself. “There’s something so tasteful to their sound selection,” Rellosa says. His preferred Loftie track is called “Redwoods,” which he describes as a “calming woodsy vibe that actually sounds like a tranquil forest rather than some canned recording.” I’ve tested the Loftie too and agree with Rellosa — the sounds do have a “high end” feel to them, compared to run-of-the-mill sound-machine options. You’ll find a variety of sound-bowl meditations, an entire rainbow of ambient noise (white, red, pink, gray, blue, brown), guided meditations, and breath work (Loftie provides samples of some of its calming sounds on its website). Rellosa is a fan of the sound bowls, saying he feels like he’s in a temple while listening to them. Even the nature sounds convey a feeling of authenticity. You can also connect your phone to the clock via Bluetooth to stream any audio you want through the speakers.

On top of the excellent sound-machine capabilities the Loftie offers, it’s a great alarm clock. It offers a similarly excellent range of wake-up sounds in its catalogue, which help rouse you with ease rather than with the panic traditional alarms can induce. It has an optional nightlight feature as well, which casts a subtle ambient glow. And for the design-minded, the clock looks great on any nightstand — especially if paired with the Loftie Lamp.

Sound type and variety: Mechanical white noise with 10 volume levels | Power source: DC adapter plug Size:  11.25” x 7” x 11.75” | Notable features: Fan, app controls

The Snooz Breez is a two-in-one fan and mechanical white-noise machine. Unlike sleeping with a traditional box fan — as many people do for the white noise and airflow it provides — the Breez lets you independently adjust the noise and airflow levels via two internal fans. Each fan has ten levels, and I like being able to run a fairly loud white-noise setting while keeping the fan low since I tend to run cold at night.

The Breez is simple to control with a touchpad panel on the front as well as an optional app you can use to create a schedule, set the fan to turn on when your room reaches a specific temperature, or simply use like a remote control. Of course, you can easily just buy a desk fan and a mechanical white-noise machine (like the Dohm) for far less than the cost of the Breez, but if you want a more aesthetically pleasing option, are low on space, or crave the more precise levels the Breez provides for sound and airflow, it’s a nifty — albeit expensive — gadget.

Sound type and variety: 288 nature sounds with sound mixing | Power source: AC power and battery | Size:  8.25” x 5.75” x 6.5” | Notable features: Bluetooth connectivity, radio, clockface

By far the most expensive option on this list, the S-6000 is the Rolls Royce of sound machines, featuring more sounds than all the others on this list combined, and is designed for those with hearing problems. Audiologist Ben Thompson recommends Sound Oasis’s devices for his tinnitus patients because of their high-quality audio, which has more in common with a professional speaker system than a cheap, tinny product. “This is the one that we can recommend to our patients who come in asking questions about sound machines for the evening and sleep,” says Thompson. Users can also use bass and treble controls to home in on their exact sound preferences.

entry.title: I Finally Found a Wireless Bra With Underwire-Level Support
entry.summary: You know that cliché about needing to take your bra off the second you get home? I don’t ever feel the need to rip this thing off.
entry.content:
I long ago resigned myself to the fact that my DD breasts would be forever confined to underwire bras that never quite fit right. Yes, I got measured. Yes, I used the size calculator from A Bra That Fits. Yes, I was wearing the correct size. And yet, I couldn’t escape the extremely unpleasant feeling of underwire digging into my ribcage whenever I put on a bra. When the pandemic hit and everyone was going hard for bralettes, I tried a couple of them and my boobs were like, “Haha ha, we cannot be contained!,” and back to underwire I went.

Until I tried The Perfect Bra from Body by Julia, which is the wireless bra I had been waiting for my whole life. Body by Julia is the shapewear company founded by Julia Haart, and if you know that name, it’s probably because you watched her reality show, My Unorthodox Life, of which the premise was essentially “woman who had grown up very sheltered and ultra-Orthodox, including being married at 19 and having four children becomes fabulously wealthy, runs a multinational corporation, and lives a Real Housewives–esque life in Tribeca with her Italian Swiss husband.” High jinks ensue.

Sadly, much like many a Housewife, Haart’s fairy-tale marriage ended in acrimonious divorce, and, not for the first time in her life, she needed to reinvent herself — so naturally, in 2023, she started a shapewear company. When I first heard about Body By Julia, I have to admit I was skeptical. Haart herself is extremely skinny (what does she know from shapewear?) and I found her television persona off-putting, to put it mildly. But I was intrigued by the range of sizes — from XS A/B to 3X E/F — and its promise of support while also being wireless. As I think most people with breasts bigger than a C cup would tell you, it’s not that we want to be wearing a bra all the time; it’s that it’s actually physically uncomfortable not to be wearing one. That was the fatal flaw of so many wireless bras and bralettes that had come before — zero coverage and zero support. I might as well be wearing pasties.

When it arrived, I was sold immediately. For one thing, the support it promised is real — my breasts don’t look saggy in clothes, and it feels like I’m actually wearing something that keeps them comfortably contained. I also appreciate that it has adjustable straps; a previous contender for a passable wireless bra, the Spanx Bra-llelujah, has straps that don’t adjust, and for my narrow shoulders, this was a must. (The Bra-llelujah also only comes in sizes XS–XL, which means nothing really fits the way it’s supposed to.) You know that cliché about needing to take your bra off the second you get home from work? Well, besides the fact that I work from home, I don’t ever feel the need to rip this thing off. If I needed to, I could sleep in it, no problem.

My one quibble with this bra is that it comes in only two colors, beige and bronze. Skims bras come in a minimum six shades — Body By Julia, let’s expand that shade range and get these bras out to everyone! The people deserve them.

entry.title: Our Favorite Montessori-Style Tools for Cooking With Kids
entry.summary: All the prep tools, furniture, tableware, and more we’ve used successfully with children at home and in the classroom.
entry.content:
We love cooking with children — even (maybe especially!) with very young, unpredictable toddlers — and we believe that any parent can, too. We also know that in every egg messily cracked, carrot scrubbed, and cookie rolled, there are huge benefits, not just to children but to parents and the connection between them.

Though we’re both raising young children ourselves, our careers have been quite different: Junnifa is an AMI-trained Montessori teacher; the founder of Fruitful Orchard Montessori in Abuja, Nigeria; and the co-author of the best-selling The Parents’ Guide to Montessori series; Kristen is the author behind Food52’s Genius Recipes cookbook series living in the San Francisco Bay Area. But the best parts of our days overlap where our work comes together: cooking alongside little ones.

We’ve heard so many times from parents who want to bring their children into the kitchen but either find the potential for mess and chaos stressful, don’t think they have the time, or just aren’t sure where to begin. So we teamed up to write The Montessori Kitchen, a cookbook-meets-parenting guide with lots of pep talks, simple recipes, and activities for parents to connect with their children in the kitchen at each stage of development from pregnancy through age 6 and beyond.

Because, with some simple mind-set shifts and a better understanding of what will engage and thrill children at various ages, sharing the kitchen with even the youngest ones can look very different: It can turn into a place of discovery and growth, helping them strengthen everything from fine motor skills to language and math concepts to patience and resilience — all from sorting through beans and waiting for the oven to beep!

Having a handful of accessible, child-size tools to welcome them in and bring order and predictability to the kitchen can also make a world of difference. Below are the tools that we’ve seen work best for small hands and bodies, both at home and in the classroom, and have made the kitchen the most rewarding place for us to parent.

A sturdy learning tower acts just like a wooden chair pulled up to the counter, giving little ones access to the same cooking surface as you, with a little more structure and peace of mind. This one has a small footprint, even tucking underneath the counter, and as your child grows you can adjust the height (and they can use the low handles to start dragging it from the sink to the fridge to the high cereal cabinet).

In Montessori classrooms, aprons aren’t just used for messier projects but each time children cook, as a marker to let them know the beginning and end of the process. Junnifa likes to start her youngest students with aprons like these that close with a Velcro strip, then move on to snaps, hooks, buttons, and finally ties as they get older and work on each skill. She also offers them two-sided aprons to begin the cooking process with an empowering choice. (Would you like the elephants or the flowers today?)

Simple baking recipes like cookies and quick breads are a good place to start cooking together, since measuring and mixing can usually happen at any pace, away from heat and sharp objects. Baking also casually introduces math, science, and literacy from an early age. These measuring cups reinforce fractions visually and really drive home the whole half-cup, quarter-cup concept.

Young children don’t quite have an understanding of time yet. Visual timers — a sand or fraction timer — help them quantify what is still an abstract idea and build patience. They can watch the sand, the liquid, or the size of the fraction gradually reduce until it is time to take out the tea bag or knead the dough.

While some tools already in your kitchen might fit comfortably in a child’s hands, look out for the ones that are unwieldy or frustrating for them to maneuver. Invest in a few just-their-size versions, like this masher that can squish not just potatoes but guacamole, refried beans, banana-bread batter, fruit compotes, and applesauce, too.

High-reward unitaskers like egg slicers and apple cutters are worth the drawer space. They build concentration and offer simple, repeatable processes to engage a child (mesmerize them, really), all while building hand strength and dexterity. This orange juicer is especially good for toddlers and young children who are in a period where they want to exert maximum effort and see the results.

It may feel instinctual to give a child a blunt knife, but it can actually be more dangerous because they end up using more force. Junnifa likes to progress children through a series of crinkle cutters that they can first use with two hands working together (the Tellashun), then one hand (the Joie), then two hands working separately as a sort of pre-knife.

She also likes a spreader with a serrated edge that can go beyond smearing PB&Js to double as a first knife for slicing soft foods like tomatoes and mozzarella. Choose what action best fits your child’s level (or try a few), always observing to make sure they’re using them safely.

A low table and chairs — also called a weaning table and chairs — are a big part of the Montessori philosophy to encourage eating independently but are also useful as food-prep surfaces and for drawing, writing, and countless craft projects. Because this table is designed to grow with children, Junnifa was able to use the same one for all four of hers. Her daughters still have it in their room as a work table.

This weaning chair allows children to sit with feet flat on the floor — important for safe self-feeding — and is stable but light enough that a child can start moving it themselves very early. They also make great step stools. Junnifa has lent them to extended family members when they had babies for 13 years and counting.

Famously and controversially, Montessori schools use real glasses and ceramic dishes, even in younger classrooms. They choose materials that won’t shatter but instead break into a few pieces. The children naturally learn from the consequence, unlike with bouncy silicone and plastic plates.

Instead of pouring water directly into children’s cups at mealtime, teachers set out small pitchers that little ones can manage themselves to refill their own cups again and again. Over time, they hone the skills of pouring and self-control as they learn to stop before the cup runs over. Outside mealtime, teachers also leave out small cups and a water dispenser at an accessible height, with a bowl or basin on the floor to catch drips (and mark the spot where children should hold the cup).

Bowls or plates with raised sides, rather than flat plates, are easier for small children to scoop against. Ramekins, which don’t shatter and are heavy enough that they don’t easily slide around, are good options for eating and serving, too.

Real silverware, sized for small hands, communicates respect and the feel of its weight invites care.

Meals in Montessori classrooms are served family-style with serving bowls and utensils that children can use successfully. They learn to identify how much they can eat and practice passing the bowl and returning the serving spoon or tongs to the dish (without licking them first).

Placemats with every utensil clearly marked serve as a cue that it’s time to eat and allow children to participate meaningfully at home by learning how to set the table for everyone, all through what is essentially a matching game.

We often think of the functional parts of eating, but young children are absorbing everything, including beauty and detail. Fresh flowers picked during a walk together and tucked into a small vase or a piece of art hung at their eye level can be a lovely, special part of meals.

When you open up the world of measuring and stirring and pouring (and the growing independence that comes along with it), messes will happen. Provide tools for cleaning up — like small dustpans, plenty of absorbent cloths, and adjustable mops (skip the disposable cloths and use a small towel) — and don’t make a big deal about it, and you’re indirectly teaching how to deal with the hard messes of life. You just clean up!

entry.title: I Found the Comfiest Socks for All Types of Boots
entry.summary: How to solve the problem of socks that scrunch up.
entry.content:
In our advice column, “Ask the Strategist,” we take your most burning shopping questions and survey friends, call up experts, and draw on our own personal experience to answer them. If you have an online-shopping question of your own, please send it to strategist@nymag.com with the subject “Ask the Strategist.” We’re here to help.

I get it. In the winter, like many city dwellers, I live in Blundstones. They’re bar none the most comfortable pair of shoes I own, but wear them with the wrong socks and suddenly they become the worst. A standard multipack of crew socks isn’t going to cut it; you’re going to spend all day tugging to keep them from bunching up in the heel. You need socks that hug your feet without feeling constrictive, and the more breathable the better. Styles like Blundstones require something more utilitarian, while dressier boots feel and look better with thinner, daintier socks. Below, the best socks for all types of (non-hiking) boots, from ankle socks to knee-highs, including ones you hide in your shoes and others you want to show off.

The socks I look for first are from Paka. They are made of 40 percent baby-alpaca fiber, 8 percent Tencel, 50 percent polyester, and 2 percent spandex. They are soft and durable and feel nice and fitted on my feet thanks to the ribbed arch support. They have a cushioned sole and toe but never feel too thick or bulky and are still so warm and breathable. I’ve owned a version of the brand’s Essential Crew Socks for 19 months, and they’re still going strong with no visible wearing out at the heel or anywhere else.

I also love my Smartwool socks. I’ve had a pair of the Everyday Margarita for over five years, and they have held up beautifully. Their composition is 52 percent merino wool, 44 percent nylon, and 4 percent elastane, and they have a similar feel, though they are not cushioned. These socks are thinner and not as padded as the Paka and feel less soft, but they are another durable option. In general, alpaca is warmer than merino, so I might choose the Pakas over the Smartwools in very cold temperatures, but I honestly couldn’t tell you the difference in warmth.

My fellow Strategist senior writers Liza Corsillo and Michael Zhao both recommend Darn Tough socks for wearing with their everyday boots. Like the Smartwool, they are made with merino wool, nylon, and elastane. Corsillo likes the basic lifestyle socks — which don’t come with cushioning but have arch support — for being “not bulky” and wears them with her Blundstones and lace-up combat boots from Sézane.

Zhao likes wearing the mid-calf cushioned lightweight socks from Darn Tough with a dressier boot from R.M.Williams or Viberg Navvy. Unlike the basic Lifestyles above, these have cushioning in the sole and below the heel as well as arch support. (Zhao says these socks are “a bit too thick to be real dress socks in dress shoes, but they are perfect for wearing with a dressier boot.”)

Corsillo says her Darn Toughs are not necessarily worn to be seen. When she does want her socks to show, she opts for Uniqlo’s men’s Colorful 50 socks. They stay on and come in, as the product name suggests, 50 different colors. Made with a cotton blend, the combination of acrylic, polyester, nylon, and spandex varies on the color.

When I’m not wearing merino wool or alpaca socks, I usually just go with cotton socks. My favorites to wear with my Blundstones are ones from Aritzia and Le Bon Shoppe. Aritzia’s ankle socks are made with 80 percent cotton, have ribbed cuffs, and are nice and thick. They hug my feet and always stay on. (Aritzia’s TNA crew socks are another Strategist favorite.)

I have both the boyfriend (crew) and girlfriend (ankle) styles and love how thick and plush they are. Made with 85 percent cotton, they have built-in arch support, a breathable-mesh top-of-the-foot part, and a ribbed cuff with retro stripes. They also come in dozens of bright colors.

Zhao also recommends these socks from Falke. He loves the ankle-height version for everyday, but for boots, he suggests trying the knee-highs. “They are as richly colored as any cotton sock, but the added merino for moisture management is particularly useful for leather boots,” he says. Zhao calls them “a fancier, more comfortable Uniqlo 50 sock” that also comes in dozens of colors. He says they’re great for non-winter boots, as they are really light and “easy to fit into a dress shoe of any kind, even loafers.” They are made with merino wool on the outside and cotton on the inside.

For dressier boots that fit closer to the foot, like my patent-leather boots from Loq or combat boots from Church’s, I need a thinner sock. These crew socks from Uniqlo are made with polyester, nylon, and spandex and feel more like tights material. They have a thicker cuff that ensures the socks stay on — and prevents the opening of ankle boots from rubbing against your skin. I can wear these with loafers and brogues too.

I wear these longer crew socks from Hue a lot as well. They are made of a polyester, rayon, and spandex blend and feel a little slippier than cotton and wool socks (similar to the Uniqlo socks above) — that helps with boots that are tighter and have less give. Sometimes I’ll wear these over tights as added cushioning and protection with dressier or heeled boots.

Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen, who recently tested a bunch of tall riding boots, prefers wearing Maggie’s Organics crew socks, which are also the Strategist’s Best in Class pick for women’s white socks. “I love them since they are thicker and prevent my feet from getting blisters,” she says. She usually wears these socks over leggings or under jeans, then boots over that. Goertzen recommends getting them in a darker color so the boot doesn’t stain them. They are made with 98 percent organic cotton that has some stretch and are plush with a ribbed cuff that keeps them in place.

I recently tried these boot socks from Hue and was pleased with them when I wore them with my 16-inch Durango Crush western boots. Those boots have a pointed toe and a 2.5-inch heel, so I was worried about wearing socks that were too thick, but both the Bubbled style and the pointelle socks worked well. The bubbled style (made of mostly polyester) feels like a cozy, fuzzy sock — really soft and plush — but not too thick. They stay up surprisingly well and were good for the breaking-in period with the cowboy boots, which are on the stiffer side, and were not noticeably sweaty. I don’t have notes on durability yet, but if my other Hue socks are any indication as to quality, I am not worried about them.

The pointelle socks are thinner and have more breathability thanks to the composition of the material (58 polyester, 26 acrylic, 12 nylon, and 4 wool) and the stitching in the cuff. They also worked well with the Durangos, staying up with no bunching. I would choose these for looks if I were to wear them with lower boots.

I would try these with my riding boots. They are they knee-high version of Corsillo’s crew socks above and come in a couple of netural colors. I liked the ribbed design that makes them look preppy (and could work well with loafers too).

Next on my to-try list are these wool-and-cashmere socks from Calzedonia. I have a couple of pairs of crew socks in this blend that I wear with dressier shoes, and I imagine the knee-high length would be great for tall boots as well.

entry.title: 37 Last-Minute Gifts for Achy People
entry.summary: From a neck stretcher beloved by opera singers to nice-looking compression gloves.
entry.content:
All I want for Christmas is to crack every joint in my back.
